articles.title: China deploys forces to monitor US warship in South China Sea - Aaj English TV
articles.summary: China deploys forces to monitor US warship in South China Sea  Aaj English TV
articles.full_text:
3 min read
China’s military said on Tuesday it had sent forces to watch a US warship that “illegally” entered waters around a disputed shoal in the South China Sea, while further north in the waterway, Taiwan reported a standoff with a Chinese vessel.
China views almost all of the South China Sea as its own territory, despite overlapping claims by Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam, with recent tension most pronounced between Beijing and Manila.
The Chinese military’s Southern Theatre Command said the USS Charleston “illegally intruded” into waters adjacent to Sabina Shoal in the Spratly Islands without Chinese government approval in the early hours of Tuesday.
“The US action infringes upon China’s sovereign rights and interests, jeopardises maritime security, and is detrimental to regional peace and stability,” it said in a statement.
“The US side should immediately cease such activities.”
China’s navy dispatched forces to track and monitor the ship, it added.
The US Navy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It generally refers to such missions as “freedom of navigation operations”, though its last known one in the South China Sea was more than a year ago.
A Philippine military spokesperson said the US ship “did not trespass into ‘Chinese territory’,” adding that no nation had the authority to require prior permission for “lawful transit through international waters.”
Last month, a China Coast Guard vessel rammed a Philippine boat on a refuelling mission near the same shoal, according to the Philippine Coast Guard. China blamed the collision on the Philippine side.
China and the Philippines, which has a mutual defence treaty with the US, both contest sovereignty over Sabina Shoal and the entire Spratly Islands archipelago.
Pratas standoff
In a separate incident on Tuesday at the top end of the South China Sea, Taiwan’s Coast Guard said a Chinese Coast Guard ship had entered restricted waters near the Taiwan-controlled Pratas Islands.
The Taiwan Coast Guard said its ship, the “Taichung”, was dispatched to warn away the Chinese boat, while both sides broadcast messages to each other.
The Chinese ship broadcast that “the so-called Republic of China does not exist”, referring to Taiwan’s official name, while the Taiwanese ship broadcast back that “the Republic of China, Taiwan, is a sovereign and independent country”, Taiwan’s Coast Guard said, adding the standoff was continuing.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The office said last week that Taiwan must “bear the consequences” of its Coast Guard using a water cannon against a Chinese fishing boat near the Pratas.
The Pratas Islands lie roughly between southern Taiwan and Hong Kong, but are only lightly defended, and security is the responsibility of Taiwan’s Coast Guard.
China has also been stepping up coast guard activity around Taiwan, including off the island’s east coast, causing concern in Western capitals.
China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory.
Speaking at a forum in Taipei on Tuesday, the chair of a review commission appointed by the US Congress said Chinese coast guard patrols to the east of Taiwan were “highly destabilising”.
Addressing the same event, Taiwan’s National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu said China had no legal claim to the waters off the island’s east.

articles.title: Nobel Peace Laureate Navi Pillay on ICC, Gaza, Rape as War Crime, Her South African Roots & Mandela - Democracy Now!
articles.summary: Nobel Peace Laureate Navi Pillay on ICC, Gaza, Rape as War Crime, Her South African Roots & Mandela  Democracy Now!
articles.full_text:
We speak with the acclaimed South African human rights lawyer and international jurist Navi Pillay, who was awarded this year’s Nobel Peace Prize. Pillay has been the United Nations high commissioner for human rights and a judge at both the International Criminal Court and at an international tribunal investigating the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. Most recently, she led the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry that concluded Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Hours after Pillay was announced as winner of the Nobel Prize, the United States imposed sweeping new sanctions against the International Criminal Court.
“It’s extremely shocking to me, totally unacceptable, that the United States administration can today impose sanctions against the International Criminal Court,” says Pillay, speaking to Democracy Now! from The Hague.
Navi Pillay is now 85 years old. She was born into an Indian Tamil family in apartheid South Africa in 1941. The first woman to start a law practice in Natal, South Africa, in 1967, Pillay began her legal career defending anti-apartheid activists including Nelson Mandela, exposing torture, and helping establish key rights for prisoners on Robben Island. Mandela, as president, later appointed Pillay to the High Court of South Africa, making her the first woman of color on that bench.
Transcript
AMY GOODMAN: Later in the broadcast, we’re going to talk about a ballot initiative here in California, which would be, if passed, the first billionaires’ wealth tax. But first, we begin today’s show with this year’s Nobel Peace Prize winner, the South African human rights lawyer, international jurist Navi Pillay. Speaking in Oslo earlier this month, the chair of the Nobel Committee announced the award.
JØRGEN WATNE FRYDNES: This year’s laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted. The Norwegian Nobel Committee has decided to award the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.
AMY GOODMAN: The Nobel Prize Committee said it chose Navi Pillay as this year’s Nobel Peace Prize winner to, quote, “issue a reminder” at a time when “judges and institutions of international law are under political attack,” unquote.
Navi Pillay has served as the United Nations high commissioner for human rights and a judge at both the International Criminal Court and at an international tribunal investigating the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. Most recently, she led the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Navi Pillay was in Nuremberg, Germany, at an annual conference of human rights lawyers and judges when she heard the news.
NAVI PILLAY: Thank you very much. Thank you very much. If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump. … The last thing I did is the delivery of the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide.
AUDIENCE MEMBER: Yeah! Bravo!
AMY GOODMAN: Hours after Navi Pillay was announced as winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, the U.S. imposed sweeping new sanctions against the International Criminal Court that target the institution as a whole. Earlier U.S. sanctions targeted individual ICC judges and court personnel. This is U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
SECRETARY OF STATE MARCO RUBIO: President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans. And that’s why today the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us, because our message is clear: The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.
AMY GOODMAN: Soon after winning the Nobel Prize, Navi Pillay visited her former colleagues at the ICC in The Hague in a show of solidarity.
Navi Pillay is now 85 years old. She was born into an Indian Tamil family in apartheid South Africa, the first woman to start a law practice in Natal, South Africa, in 1967. She began her legal career defending anti-apartheid activists including Nelson Mandela, another Nobel Peace Prize winner, exposing torture, and helping establish key rights for prisoners on Robben Island.
To talk more about her remarkable career, from apartheid South Africa to serving on the International Criminal Court, findings of genocide from Rwanda to Gaza, and President Trump’s attacks on international law, we are joined now by the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay, joining us today from The Hague in the Netherlands.
Navi Pillay, welcome to Democracy Now! It’s great to have you with us. Congratulations on winning this global peace prize. If you could respond to its significance and also talk about the significance of you hearing the news when you were in Nuremberg, Germany, so seminal when it came to the establishment of international law so many decades ago after World War II? Congratulations again!
NAVI PILLAY: Thank you so much, Amy. I’m really pleased to be on your program. You know, the discovery now is — I mean, Democracy Now! is well known. I hope you would include my country sometimes. It’s a extremely valuable program. I’m really happy to be on the program.
And to your questions, yes, I’m now at the International Court of Justice. I serve as ad hoc judge in one of the cases. I came to do some work here. And this was a big surprise to me. I was attending, as you’ve just told the audience, that I was attending a conference in Nuremberg in Courtroom 600, when someone shouted — it was Stephen Rapp, an American, actually, the previous U.S. war crimes investigator, and he announced from his cellphone that that’s the news. And, of course, I had not heard from the committee, so I was astonished, and I disbelieved them, until I heard the announcement myself later online. And it turned out that they had been trying to get hold of me, but there was no connection in the inside the courtroom. A wonderful surprise.
Part of the reasons why I was skeptical is, firstly, because we don’t often hear of them giving the award to women. They have given — mine, apparently, is the 21st woman out of 100-some-odd — 90 were men — recipients. So, that was one factor. And the other is, yes, you know, judges and lawyers don’t often get awards, especially not judges. We work quietly in our courtrooms. We speak through the judgments. And we don’t act it out or make speeches thereafter.
For me, the significance of the fact that I was in Courtroom 600, where the Nazis were tried, is very important, because as an 18-year-old, when I was studying in apartheid South Africa, I was studying law, and nonwhite students attended the university separately, in separate facilities, which in our case happened to be a potato warehouse, and I found these copies of the Nuremberg judgments. Nobody else had seen them. They were high up. I climb a ladder, find some of them. And that started my interest in international justice, because in my country the laws were bad. They were immoral. Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher had used the veto to stop U.N. sanctions against apartheid South Africa. Of course, later, they were pressured by civil society to change and not use the vote, so sanctions were applied, and all of which contributed to ending apartheid. So, I was very interested in us having some access to international justice or a system of laws that had values and principles behind them.
And the significance of Nuremberg is, of course, it was mainly a U.S. idea. The person who is always quoted when it comes to the Nuremberg trials is Justice Jackson, who was a United States person. And all of us have learned about Nuremberg through his writings. So, here’s a country so highly committed to international justice, opting to use the rule of law rather than force in dealing with the high-level Nazi criminals. It was such a wonderful idea. All of us lawyers and judges subscribe to that.
And therefore, it’s extremely shocking to me, totally unacceptable, that the United States administration can today impose sanctions against the International Criminal Court. Straight from Nuremberg, I came to The Hague and went to that court to show solidarity with the staff. These sanctions affect all the staff, who are doing such a courageous job in their investigations.
Now, I don’t want to jump too much, but if I may just add that if the objection is that the judges authorize the prosecution to investigate not only the Taliban’s activities but also the activities of U.S. soldiers who were based in Afghanistan at that time, so if the objection is to the ICC even thinking or considering of investigating those U.S. soldiers, the solution for U.S. is simple: You begin investigating, because the ICC statute doesn’t allow that court to intervene as long as the state is investigating, prosecuting these crimes.
JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Navi Pillay, you chaired the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territories from 2021 to 2025, and as soon as you got news of the Nobel Peace Prize award, you mentioned the decision of the commission there in terms of the genocide committed by Israel in Gaza. Why did you feel it was so necessary to immediately refer to that, especially?
NAVI PILLAY: You know, as I said, I work very well with the U.S. I chaired commissions of inquiry that the U.S. supported, such as two in respect of North Korea. So I know that Americans support the principle of ending impunity for these serious crimes and that they support justice and accountability.
I mentioned the Gaza report because it has been widely covered, and I’ve been accused of being biased and taking sides and speaking lies. That report was mandated by the United Nations Human Rights Council, so it’s a U.N. body. We followed all the U.N. rules, and we worked in cooperation with all the U.N. agencies

articles.title: Europe is preparing for direct talks with Putin, FT reports. One possible proposal: Russia gets Donbas, Ukraine gets NATO membership. - Meduza
articles.summary: Europe is preparing for direct talks with Putin, FT reports. One possible proposal: Russia gets Donbas, Ukraine gets NATO membership.  MeduzaThe Future of Russian-European Relations Is Bleak  Carnegie Endowment for International PeaceNATO gegen Russland: Überlegenheit auf dem Papier, Verwundbarkeit in der Wirklichkeit  Xpert.Digital - Konrad WolfensteinEurope is considering two scenarios for ending the war in Ukraine, according to the Financial Times  UA.N...
articles.full_text:
European leaders are rethinking their approach to the Kremlin, Financial Times foreign affairs columnist Gideon Rachman writes. More politicians in the European Union now agree that negotiations with Vladimir Putin should not remain the exclusive prerogative of the United States. European countries could soon open their own talks with the Kremlin. Channels of communication are already in place, he says.
EU policy toward Russia has rested on two main pillars until now: support for Ukraine and sanctions. European leaders have tried to shape the negotiations by influencing Donald Trump’s position, but those efforts are growing less effective. Europe also fears Trump is more interested in business deals with Moscow than in security issues.
In any direct talks, Putin could be offered two options for ending the war, Rachman writes: freezing the conflict along the front line in exchange for a guarantee that Ukraine will not join NATO, or ceding all of the Donbas to Moscow’s control, after which Kyiv could join the alliance.
Meanwhile, relations between Kyiv and Washington are going through a new crisis, triggered by an energy crisis and Trump’s push to lower diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections to Congress.
Trump has repeatedly urged Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries and declare an energy truce. After diplomatic failure, he struck a deal with Moscow on diesel supplies. Volodymyr Zelensky said the United States had “chosen the side” of Russia. Trump responded that it was easier for him to reach an agreement with Putin than with Zelensky, adding that Ukraine needs to hold elections.
Relations between the two leaders are at their “lowest point” since the clash in the Oval Office in 2025, the WSJ writes. The latest exchange took place a day earlier: Trump accused Zelensky of not wanting to end the war, while Zelensky said Ukraine is being pressured to capitulate.
Amid this, U.S. Vice President JD Vance has spoken out against Ukraine joining NATO: “We don’t have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They’re not in NATO. I don’t think that they should be in NATO,” he said. Vance also refused to call Kyiv an ally of Washington, saying they have “divergent interests from time to time.”

Residents of Komyshuvakha, a front-line village in the Zaporizhzhia region, are being evacuated because of the threat of Russian drone strikes. These photos were taken October 19, 2026.

articles.summary: Trump admin sees escalating risk from Houthis, prompting unprecedented wave of warnings  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and VideosU.S. ramps up warnings to Americans in Middle East after deadly Houthi strikes  CBS NewsSecurity Alert: U.S. Embassy Amman – October 18, 2026  U.S. Embassy in Jordan (.gov)US issues rare Middle East red alert warning to its citizens in the region  EuronewsUS warns Americans in Middle East to exercise ‘heightened vigilance...

source_detail.name: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos

articles.full_text:
Concern comes as Saudi Arabia has struggled to defend against Houthi attacks.
The Trump administration now assesses that Houthi attacks pose a broad, escalating threat to Americans in the Middle East, prompting an unprecedented decision by the State Department to issue urgent warnings about the Iranian-backed rebel group across a dozen countries in the region, U.S. officials told ABC News.
While the department has been notifying U.S. nationals in Saudi Arabia about the risk of Houthi attacks for weeks, U.S. embassies in Bahrain, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar and the UAE issued coordinated security alerts on Sunday, advising Americans that hostilities involving Houthi militants "have the potential to escalate rapidly" beyond areas that have been impacted so far.
The U.S. mission to Yemen and its virtual embassy for Iran also issued identical messages.
"We are actively warning U.S. citizens about the very real threat the Houthis pose and urging them to heed official guidance. These alerts are part of a proactive effort by the Trump administration to ensure Americans are aware of potential risks," State Department Deputy Assistant Secretary for Press Edgar Vasquez said in a statement to ABC News.
The heightened concern comes as Saudi Arabia has struggled to defend against deadly missile and drone strikes on energy and aviation targets, such as an attack on Riyadh's main international airport earlier this month that claimed that killed 13 people, including an American citizen.
The U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia has been issuing near-daily alerts to Americans traveling in the country, advising on Monday that they should "be aware of potential attacks on airports, airspace closures, flight cancellations, and travel disruptions" and "take extreme caution if you choose to use airports in Saudi Arabia."
Saudi Arabia has also displayed signs of growing alarm, postponing a major annual investment conference commonly referred to as "Davos in the Desert" due to the security environment.
While Saudi-led forces have carried out significant air and ground operations against the Houthis in Yemen, these campaigns have not curtailed incoming attacks. On Monday, a spokesperson for the rebel group claimed it launched multiple strikes against Saudi targets.
Riyadh is actively trying to court regional support for its fight against the Houthis, and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman previously appealed to President Trump for support.
The U.S. has been providing Saudi Arabia with significant targeting assistance and intelligence support. But so far Trump has declined to order direct U.S. military intervention, as sources say the administration has been wary of opening a second front in the Middle East while the conflict with Iran remains unsettled.
Last week, Trump told ABC News that the Houthis were "behaving very badly," but did not say whether he would change his mind on ordering strikes against the rebel group.
The Houthis are a Shiite political and military organization that took form as an opposition force to the Yemeni government.
In 2011, the Houthis played a major role in sparking the Yemeni Revolution, which was born out of a wave of anti-government protests and uprisings known as the Arab Spring.
The revolution forced a transfer of power, but the Houthis were displeased with the newly installed leaders and in 2014 the group took control of Sanaa, the Yemeni capital, prompting an ongoing civil war that has ravaged the country.
A Saudi-led coalition first intervened in the conflict in 2015 with the stated goal of restoring the former rulers to power. A UN-brokered truce was reached in 2022, resulting in relative calm until mid-2026.
Amid broader regional tensions, the Houthis resumed attacks against Saudi Arabia in July. In September, the group launched a ground campaign that resulted in significant initial territorial gains across western Yemen, triggering a counter-offensive by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

articles.title: US gave us no warning of Russian strikes on Kyiv power plants, Zelenskyy says | Ukraine - The Guardian
articles.summary: US gave us no warning of Russian strikes on Kyiv power plants, Zelenskyy says | Ukraine  The GuardianUkrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC  BBCZelenskiy says Ukraine got no warning as Russian missiles rain in  ReutersUS gave Kyiv just 60 seconds’ warning of ballistic missile attack  The Telegraph‘Tell that to the families’: Polish FM hits back at Hegseth over Afghanistan remarks  TVP World
articles.full_text:
Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, reviving concerns that Washington is withholding intelligence to bully Kyiv into capitulating to Moscow.
Yuri Ihnat, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian air force, said on television on Monday morning that Ukraine had not received a warning before a Russian missile barrage hit power plants in Kyiv at about 11pm. Earlier, a Ukrainian government official had told the Guardian the US had not warned the capital about the impending missile strike.
Ukraine did receive a warning before a subsequent strike, at 3am, Ihnat added.
“Once again, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack in multiple waves throughout the night, and once again, there was no warning from our partners,” Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post on Monday morning.
“When the supply of missiles for Ukrainian air defence is blocked, and Russia receives sanctions relief or delays, it is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners,” the president added.
Zelenskyy is grappling with recent US moves benefiting the Russian president, Vladimir Putin.
On Friday, Donald Trump waived a sweeping package of sanctions on Russia, telling Congress the pause on the legislation, named after the late senator Lindsey Graham and passed by both chambers, was in the national interest. Ukraine has also complained of slowed deliveries of PAC-3 air defence missiles from the US.
The US president wrote on Truth Social on Sunday: “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.
“Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”
Trump also told reporters on Monday that he would consider a trilateral meeting with Russia and China. He said: “We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation. If President Xi wants to have it, I’d have it.”
For years, the US has warned Ukraine before Russia launched ballistic missiles, giving authorities several minutes to sound alarms and allow civilians to reach shelters before the strikes hit. However, Ukraine has said it was not warned on at least three days in the past week before missiles were launched, amid a public quarrel between Zelenskyy and Trump.
Speaking in the early hours of Monday on a trip to Samarkand, Uzbekistan, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “If it happened last night, I don’t know exactly. I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system.”
US officials have not previously mentioned a software glitch in the early warning system. In at least one case, Ukrainian officials had been told that bad weather over southern Russia had obscured preparations for the missile launch. Rubio said the military’s European Command was looking into the strikes.
The US has maintained plausible deniability as services and programmes provided to support Ukraine have suddenly begun to fail. The Trump administration has denied that it throttled services in Ukraine for Starlink, the satellite internet service run by Elon Musk that is used both on offensive drones and anti-air weapons by Ukraine.
Ukraine has also said US weapons delivered through the PURL scheme, where Europe purchases US weapons then delivers them to Ukraine, have been delayed. The Trump administration reportedly threatened Kyiv with a slowdown in crucial weapons deliveries unless it stopped striking Russian oil refineries.
On Sunday, Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war, setting fire to an oil export terminal and a depot in St Petersburg.
The Russian barrage on Sunday evening hit 28 substations and other critical energy facilities, depriving more than 500,000 people of electricity, heat and running water, Zelenskyy said on social media. Russia has sought to disrupt daily life in Ukraine by attacking trains, shopping centres, fuel stations and supermarkets, among other sites.
Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region, Zelenskyy said, and officials in the capital reported that a 21-year-old woman had been killed.
Later drone strikes on a public park in the north-eastern Kharkiv region killed six people, including young children. The regional governor, Oleg Synegubov, said on Telegram that three of the dead in the attack on Nova Vodolaha were children, including one in a pushchair. Seven children were among the 14 wounded. Police posted pictures showing damaged playground equipment.
Synegubov condemned “another terrorist act by the Russian Federation”, saying “the enemy strikes a recreational park in the middle of the day, knowing that there is no military infrastructure there at all”.
Pope Leo XIV spoke by phone with Zelenskyy on Monday to discuss the embattled city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region, according to a Vatican statement. He told the Ukrainian president that he had asked Putin for a humanitarian ceasefire during a call with the Russian leader on Friday.
Residents of Oleshky face a worsening humanitarian crisis, with shortages of food and medication, as they are caught in the crossfire between Russian and Ukrainian troops. The Vatican said that Leo had expressed deep concern about conditions in the city and sought a ceasefire to permit aid deliveries and evacuations.
The call to Zelenskyy came two days after Leo, 71, was discharged from a hospital in Rome where he underwent a lung cancer operation on Tuesday.
The Kremlin said on Friday it had explained to Leo what it called “the Kyiv regime’s responsibility for the difficult humanitarian situation”.

Wanjun Xie, chairman of the Chinese Democratic Party, a group banned by Chinese authorities, said that Kim had been transferred to Beijing because North Korea lacked the medical facilities to treat him. He later claimed his remains had been secretly returned to his homeland.
Writing on X on Monday, he said: “His body has been secretly transported back to North Korea, and the news of his death is being kept under wraps.”
In an attempt to quell the death reports, North Korea’s state news agency released images of Kim and his teenage daughter perusing winter coats.
The agency said the photos had been taken on Monday, but this has not been independently verified.
In one photo, Kim is seen inspecting a pink shoe, while another shows him observing rolls of fabric.
The North Korean dictator’s health has long been a source of scrutiny.
In September, South Korea’s spy agency claimed he was “extremely obese” and at risk of heart disease.
In 2020, a high-profile North Korean defector claimed he was 99 per cent certain the leader had died following heart surgery before Kim appeared in public.

articles.title: Alberta rejects a move toward independence from Canada in a victory for Carney - AP News
articles.summary: Alberta rejects a move toward independence from Canada in a victory for Carney  AP NewsAlberta rejects secession referendum, chooses to remain part of Canada  CNNAlberta voters overwhelmingly reject separation process in a victory for Carney  Boston.comAlberta's decision to stay in Canada gives Carney backing to take on Trump  BBC‘I will honour this mandate’: Smith vows not to hold another referendum on separation  CP24
articles.full_text:
Alberta voters overwhelmingly reject separation process in a victory for Carney
EDMONTON, Alberta (AP) — Voters in Canada’s oil-rich Alberta province overwhelmingly backed remaining in the country, referendum results showed Tuesday, delivering a boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s push for national unity as U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and annexation threats rally Canadians around their country.
With more than 1.9 million votes counted and results reported from 90% of voting areas and locations, 75% of voters supported remaining in Canada, while 25% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.
The referendum was not a direct vote on independence. Approval would have set Alberta on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada.
“It’s a great result for Canada that Albertans have chosen unity,” Carney told reporters Tuesday before a Cabinet meeting in Ottawa.
Carney said the roughly one-quarter of voters who backed beginning the separation process did not necessarily want independence, suggesting only a smaller “hard core” favored leaving Canada. Some voters said they wanted to send Ottawa a message rather than separate.
Separatists confront defeat, Smith rules out another vote
Alberta separatist organizer David Parker acknowledged the scale of the defeat.
“Independence feels far away and we should not pretend this was not a defeat,” he wrote on social media.
In a televised address Tuesday night, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith welcomed the result and pledged not to hold another referendum on separation while she remains in office.
“Yesterday, Albertans voted overwhelmingly in favor of remaining a province of Canada,” Smith said. “The voter turnout was historic and a powerful testimony of the passion Albertans feel for our country and our province.”
Smith said Alberta would continue pressing Ottawa for greater provincial autonomy, but disputes would be settled within Canada’s political and legal institutions rather than through separation.
Carney said he spoke with Smith on Tuesday morning about the results and greater federal-provincial cooperation, including immigration.
“Don’t mess with Canada. President Trump is watching this,” Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters.
A fringe cause has become a movement that won’t disappear
Alberta, home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Canada’s federal government in Ottawa runs deep, but hasn’t traditionally translated into widespread support for independence.
Despite the overwhelming rejection, separatist leaders vowed to continue pressing for independence.
Separatist parties traditionally attracted only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Premier Jason Kenney said. Anger over COVID-19 restrictions helped mobilize activists who later embraced the separatist movement, he said.
Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have helped Carney rally support in Alberta, where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular.
At a separatist referendum night gathering at an Edmonton restaurant, the crowd fell quiet as results rolled in.
“We’re not going anywhere,” said Jeff Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project. “We’ve dominated the conversation in the last year. We’ve been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we’re going to continue moving forward.”
Rath said before the vote that he would be thrilled with 30% support. He also said he wanted Smith ousted as UCP leader and believed the party could splinter, potentially creating a new pro-independence party.
Ian Brodie, a University of Calgary political scientist and former chief of staff to Conservative Prime Minister Stephen Harper, dismissed Rath and fellow separatist organizer Mitch Sylvestre as “nobodies,” saying they failed to gain traction even in a district that elected a separatist to Alberta’s legislature in 1982.
“Even on a very soft question — whether to hold a referendum on separation — they couldn’t gain real traction,” Brodie said.
A referendum on a referendum
Edmonton voter Shawn Campbell said he voted to begin the separation process even though he doesn’t want Alberta to leave Canada.
“It sends a message to Ottawa that Albertans are not happy,” he said.
Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticized spending money on a “referendum on a referendum” rather than healthcare.
With Trump threatening Canada, Malka said, “It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united. Instead we’re fighting among ourselves.”
Edmonton resident Ali Khowaja, who immigrated to Canada six years ago, welcomed the result, saying he was glad Alberta had chosen unity rather than experiencing a Brexit-style rupture.
“Over the years, you’ve seen the consequences and what that meant,” he said. “I was concerned, especially as someone who is an immigrant to Canada.”

articles.title: United States Escalated Hostility Toward Cuba Throughout 2026 - teleSUR English
articles.summary: United States Escalated Hostility Toward Cuba Throughout 2026  teleSUR English
articles.full_text:
Flags of Cuba and the United States. Photo: TRT World
October 20, 2026 Hour: 4:41 pm
A combination of maritime fuel blockades, power grid collapses, and legal indictments deepens economic hardship across the island nation.
Since the beginning of Donald Trump’s second administration, the United States’ relentless hostility toward Cuba has been on the rise. This friction has centered on unilateral sanctions, trade restrictions, and direct legal actions against former Cuban government leaders.
RELATED:
Russia Condemns U.S. Arrest Warrant for Raul Castro
2026 brought to Cuba a series of severe economic challenges, particularly regarding its energy sector. U.S. executive orders and maritime monitoring actions aimed at restricting oil shipments to state-owned Cuban entities contributed directly to fuel shortages across the island. These restrictions affected power generation, agricultural transport, municipal services, and health sector logistics.
In May, the U.S. Department of Justice unsealed a federal jury indictment in Miami charging former Cuban President Raúl Castro and five co-defendants with conspiracy and murder related to a 1996 aerial shootdown.
Cuba Fuel Restrictions and the Energy Infrastructure Crisis
On January 29, Trump issued an executive order stating that the U.S. would impose tariffs on any country that sent oil to Cuba. The U.S. government authorized certain fuel shipments exclusively to private commercial entities, while blocking access to state-managed refineries and power facilities.
This policy created severe fuel deficits for public utilities responsible for national electricity generation. A deficit that led to recurring shutdowns across the National Electrical System. On March 16, 2026, the national grid suffered a complete collapse after a major boiler leak occurred at the Antonio Guiteras Thermoelectric Power Plant in Matanzas. By October 2026, another mechanical breakdown left up to 75 percent of the country without power.
The energy deficits extended beyond residential electricity. In February 2026, fuel shortages forced Cuban aviation authorities to suspend refuel operations for foreign air carriers. Consequently, airlines such as Air Canada, Rossiya, and Nordwind suspended flights to the island. International tourist arrivals dropped by approximately 58 percent by June 2026 compared to prior operational benchmarks.
Public sanitation and healthcare systems reported operational disruptions due to the fuel deficit. In Havana, local authorities reported that only 44 of 106 municipal collection trucks were operational in early 2026 due to empty fuel tanks.
In June 2026, United Nations human rights monitors showed a 60 percent decline in agricultural production caused by fuel shortages for farming equipment and transport vehicles.
Hybrid Operations and International Diplomatic Positions
Throughout 2026, the U.S. diplomatic campaign was accompanied by increased military surveillance, intelligence monitoring, and diplomatic warnings. Reports documented an increase in U.S. military reconnaissance flights operating over international airspace near the Cuban coastline.
Cuban defense officials countered that the frequency of these flights constituted deliberate psychological pressure and surveillance of national infrastructure.
In parallel with maritime and aerial activities, U.S. diplomats engaged with governments in Latin America and Europe to restrict economic partnerships with Havana.
The U.S. State Department urged partner nations to terminate bilateral agreements involving Cuban medical professionals. Several governments, including Guatemala, Honduras, and several Caribbean nations, subsequently reduced or phased out participation in Cuban medical exchange programs.
In August 2026, UN human rights rapporteurs released a joint statement concluding that unilateral fuel restrictions and financial blockades exacerbated severe shortages of basic goods, medicine, and food.
The Legal Prosecution of Raul Castro and the 1996 Case
On May 20, 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice unsealed a federal indictment in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida charging former Cuban President Raúl Castro and five co-defendants with conspiracy, destruction of aircraft, and four counts of murder.
The legal push escalated further on October 19, 2026, when Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced that the Office of Statewide Prosecution and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement secured a state arrest warrant for Castro, charging him with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder.
Both prosecutions center on an incident that took place on February 24, 1996, when Cuban military MiG fighter jets intercepted and shot down two civilian Cessna 337 aircraft. The planes were operated by Brothers to the Rescue (Hermanos al Rescate), a Miami-based organization founded by José Basulto.
The group initially focused on search-and-rescue operations for Cuban migrants in the Florida Straits, but later expanded its activities to include dropping political leaflets directly over Havana.
The 1996 aerial interception resulted in the deaths of four crew members: Carlos Costa, Armando Alejandre Jr., Mario de la Peña, and Pablo Morales. U.S. federal and state authorities asserted that the civilian planes were destroyed over international waters without legal justification.
Florida state prosecutors cited military chain-of-command statements from the period in which Castro, then Minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces, authorized commanders to shoot down unauthorized aircraft over the sea without prior consultation.
In response, the Cuban government stated that the civilian aircraft had repeatedly violated Cuban sovereign airspace despite official diplomatic warnings issued to the U.S. State Department prior to the incident.
Cuban authorities and foreign affairs analysts characterized the revival of thirty-year-old charges as a coordinated exercise of extraterritorial judicial power. Officials in Havana rejected the dual legal actions as politically motivated efforts to criminalize Cuba’s historical leadership and create legal grounds for continuing trade and financial sanctions.
Domestic Mobilization and Sovereign Defense
The Cuban government and civic organizations responded to the rising external pressures through formal diplomatic rejections, official government statements, and public mobilizations.
Following the unsealing of the May 2026 U.S. indictment against former President Raúl Castro, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla rejected the legal action in an address to international media and diplomats.
Rodríguez Parrilla characterized the indictment as a politically motivated maneuver designed to justify economic sanctions and interfere with Cuban domestic jurisdiction. President Miguel Díaz-Canel reiterated this position, stating that national sovereignty and historical decisions regarding territorial air defense remain non-negotiable under international law.
In urban centers across Cuba, including Havana, Santiago de Cuba, and Matanzas, civil organizations and neighborhood committees organized rallies opposing external interference and economic restrictions.
At the same time, state ministries implemented emergency measures to manage reduced fuel supplies and maintain essential public services. Municipal governments established scheduled electricity rotations, prioritized available diesel fuel for medical facilities and water distribution pumps, and expanded the use of draft animals and non-motorized transport in agricultural regions.
On the international stage, Havana received diplomatic backing from several multilateral organizations and regional governments. The Bolivarian Alliance for the Peoples of Our America (ALBA-TCP) issued a joint declaration condemning unilateral coercive measures against Cuba’s energy sector.
During the United Nations General Assembly in September 2026, representatives from non-aligned nations called for an immediate end to the trade embargo, citing its negative impact on civilian health, infrastructure, and human development.
Analysis of Coercive Strategies and Long-Term Impacts
The events of 2026 reflect an intensification of U.S. policy toward Cuba through a combination of trade restrictions, infrastructural pressure, and legal mechanisms targeting state leadership.
The strategic focus on restricting fuel imports significantly affected Cuba’s national power grid, agricultural logistics, and public transportation. Simultaneously, the unsealing of a thirty-year-old indictment against Raúl Castro added a significant legal dimension to bilateral relations.
Economic data, energy assessments, and reports from international monitors demonstrate that the primary burden of fuel deficits and infrastructure instability falls directly on the civilian population. The disruptions to medical supplies, food distribution, and municipal sanitation illustrate the direct impact of unilateral economic sanctions on daily life.
Despite persistent resource constraints and structural deficits, the Cuban government has maintained state operations and institutional control through domestic conservation strategies and international partnerships.
Sources: Granma – Juventud Rebelde – Cuba Debate – Cubavisión – CiberCuba – EcuRed – TeleSUR – BBC – CNN – The Guardian – La Radio del Sur

articles.title: Indian military mindset risks nuclear stability, warns ex-SPD chief - Pakistan Today
articles.summary: Indian military mindset risks nuclear stability, warns ex-SPD chief  Pakistan Today
articles.full_text:
LONDON: Adviser to the National Command Authority (NCA) and former director general of the Strategic Plans Division (SPD), retired Lieutenant General Mazhar Jamil, has warned that an ideology blending mythology with national power is shaping Indian military thinking and posing serious risks to nuclear stability in South Asia and beyond.
“Indian military thinking is being shaped by a dangerous ideology, which conflates mythology with national power,” he said in a keynote address at a workshop on Nuclear Deterrence and Strategic Stability in South Asia, organised by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London last week.
The institute shared a transcript of his address late on Monday.
Jamil said a region’s strategic stability depended on the political beliefs and strategic thinking of states, which shaped their policies and security environment. In South Asia’s nuclearised setting, he stressed, political engagement was essential, while military adventurism and hegemonic ambitions carried unacceptable risks.
He identified Kashmir as the central unresolved dispute between Pakistan and India, arguing that it should be settled in accordance with United Nations Security Council resolutions.
Instead, he said, India had sought to avoid a political settlement and manage the dispute through military force in Indian-administered Kashmir and aggression against Pakistan. Such an approach had failed to resolve the conflict, leaving Kashmir a persistent nuclear flashpoint that continued to undermine regional security.
Jamil argued that Indian revisionist ambitions and the belief that South Asia belonged to Hindu civilisation had contributed to a more confrontational regional outlook. He cited the display of a map of “Greater Bharat” in India’s parliament as an indication of what he described as expansionist political thinking.
He also criticised the rise of the Hindutva ideology, saying it sought to marginalise and delegitimise non-Hindu communities, particularly Muslims. This, he said, had added another layer of complexity to the region’s security environment and allowed an exclusionary nationalist outlook to influence political, military and societal institutions.
The former SPD chief warned that this ideological outlook had also penetrated Indian military thinking, creating a dangerous combination of strategic overconfidence and inadequate appreciation of nuclear realities.
Jamil said the Indian leadership needed to draw three fundamental lessons from the history of conflict and nuclear deterrence.
First, military operations and wars could not permanently resolve disputes unless they were accompanied by a political settlement. He called for a political process and dialogue to resolve the Kashmir dispute and establish lasting stability.
Second, military adventurism between nuclear-armed states could escalate a crisis without delivering meaningful policy gains. India, he said, could not impose its objectives on another nuclear power through military aggression.
The third lesson concerned the unpredictable nature of war and the risks of escalation. Citing military theorist Carl von Clausewitz, Jamil warned that conflicts often began with an assumption of control but could end with the realisation that escalation had become uncontrollable.
In South Asia, he cautioned, such a realisation could come too late to prevent a catastrophe if India continued to pursue provocation under the assumption that it could dominate escalation.
He described Pakistan and India as pursuing “two diametrically opposing strategic approaches”. According to Jamil, India sought regional dominance through revisionist political thinking, while Pakistan’s approach centred on resolving disputes politically, promoting shared prosperity and defending its sovereignty.
Jamil identified three developments in the international strategic environment that, in his assessment, had influenced Indian policy and behaviour.
The first was the wider geopolitical competition in the Asia-Pacific, in which India had presented itself as a net security provider. He argued that the United States and other Western powers had been too quick to endorse this role without adequately examining India’s political objectives and capacity, giving New Delhi what he described as a false sense of regional hegemony.
The second concerned international support for India’s technological and nuclear programmes. Jamil criticised the waiver granted to India by the Nuclear Suppliers Group, despite what he called its irresponsible nuclear behaviour.
He said India was pursuing one of the world’s fastest-growing nuclear and missile programmes without sufficient regard for arms control, a key component of strategic stability. He cited the development of intercontinental ballistic missiles and submarine-launched ballistic missiles, as well as eight nuclear reactors operating outside International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards.
India’s non-membership of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and the operation of unsafeguarded reactors, he argued, raised concerns about potential sources of fissile material for nuclear weapons.
Jamil said India’s nuclear and missile ambitions increasingly extended beyond South Asia, including into the Indian Ocean, while remaining insufficiently constrained by arms-control arrangements and transparency.
The third development, he said, was what he viewed as a policy of appeasement by some major powers, which had encouraged India to believe that its exceptional treatment would continue to be accepted internationally.
He also accused India of using propaganda and disinformation to deflect scrutiny of its human rights record in Kashmir and the treatment of minorities. He warned that any further deterioration in Indian-administered Kashmir could have serious implications for regional peace and security.
Jamil further warned that access to advanced technologies, space-based capabilities and dual-use weapons systems was complicating South Asia’s strategic environment.
Precision-guided systems and platforms capable of serving conventional as well as nuclear roles, he said, were blurring the distinction between the two categories of warfare. Given the geographical proximity of Pakistan and India, this ambiguity increased the danger of miscalculation during a crisis.
He cited the March 9, 2022, BrahMos missile incident, when a missile launched from India landed in Pakistan. Jamil said it took India 48 hours to inform its nuclear-armed neighbour and criticised New Delhi for not sharing the findings of its investigation.
Although India described the incident as accidental, he said, it raised questions about the functioning of its command-and-control systems and the possibility of unauthorised actions within its military organisation.
He also described the launch of dual-capable BrahMos missiles during the four-day conflict between Pakistan and India in May 2025 as a deliberate provocation that could have triggered a catastrophic miscalculation.
Jamil concluded that such developments made the region’s security dynamics increasingly dangerous, particularly in the absence of institutionalised confidence-building measures and an arms-control framework capable of addressing emerging technologies.

articles.summary: Egypt moves toward sending troops to Saudi Arabia to help defend against attacks by Iran-backed Houthis  CBS NewsEgyptian Lawmakers Push Back on Sisi’s Request to Send Troops to Saudi Arabia  الحرةExplainer: What's behind Egypt's move towards possible military involvement in Saudi-Yemen conflict?  ReutersWhat help can Egypt offer Saudi Arabia in the war against the Houthis?  Al JazeeraEgypt Is Inactive No More  Geopolitical Futures
articles.full_text:
Cairo - Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has asked the country's Parliament to authorize the military to help defend Saudi Arabia after Yemen's intensified their attacks on the kingdom, targeting and oil infrastructure.
Al-Sisi stressed that it would be a defensive mission and only if the kingdom requests assistance.
"Egypt will take any measures requested by Saudi Arabia to protect and defend it," al-Sisi said Saturday during a military graduation ceremony.
Under Egypt's Constitution, the president must consult the National Defense Council and obtain approval from two-thirds of Parliament before deploying the armed forces on a combat mission abroad.
On Sunday, al-Sisi chaired a meeting of the National Defense Council, which reviewed what the Egyptian presidency described as the "grave escalations unfolding in the region" and the "unacceptable attacks" against Saudi Arabia.
The council pledged to provide "all necessary and possible forms of support to the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to defend its security and stability, and to safeguard its resources, territorial integrity, and Islamic holy sites."
Egypt has managed, so far, to stay out of all the recent military conflicts in the region and has tried to de-escalate and find political solutions. For some, this is one of al-Sisi's greatest achievements.
But Samir Ragheb, a retired army brigadier and political and strategic analyst, told CBS News that it was time for Egypt to make good on commitments it had made to helping secure the region.
"Egypt has repeatedly pledged to support the security of the Gulf states and has issued numerous statements reaffirming this commitment," Ragheb said. "However, this is a time of war, not politics and statements. If Egypt fails to deliver on these promises, they will lose their meaning and amount to nothing more than empty threats."
"The Gulf states have invested billions of dollars in Egypt. Morally, it's Egypt's turn to return the favor," he said.
Parliament convened an emergency session on Sunday and was expected to approve the resolution on Tuesday, but the vote was postponed until next Monday.
The Egyptian Social Democratic Party instructed its parliamentary bloc to abstain from voting on the resolution, saying in a statement it had not received sufficient information about "the mission's scope, costs, and risks, as well as the arrangements in place to protect Egyptian forces."
Ragheb is certain the region is heading toward a more severe escalation.
"Egypt is not going to defend the kingdom against the Houthis," he said. "The threat is much bigger than the Houthis. This includes Iran, Iraqi militias and sleeper cells within the kingdom itself."
However, he also believes Egypt will lose much of its influence in the region if it doesn't intervene.
"If you want to be a regional player, you must play a role," he said. "Otherwise, you will lose your seat at the table."
Ragheb argued that the United States' in support of Saudi Arabia created a vacuum that must be filled by others. He said Egypt should take on the Arab share of that role.
Other regional powers are also trying to fill the vacuum. In August, Saudi Arabia signed a joint defense agreement with Turkey and Pakistan known as the Mecca Accords.
"Even before Saudi Arabia asked for Egyptian support, the Mecca Accords was a death certificate for the idea of relying on America for any form of defense," Ragheb said.

articles.title: The Growing Risk of Nuclear War - International Viewpoint
articles.summary: The Growing Risk of Nuclear War  International Viewpoint
articles.full_text:
MLK’s WARNING FROM nearly 60 years ago continues to be true. As psychologist Robert Lifton once wrote, vulnerability is the “central existential fact of the nuclear age” because everyone, everywhere, is “susceptible to instant destruction.” [3]
That potential for instant destruction has become more imminent, with the most militarily powerful countries adding fuel to an already overheated arms race and engaging in wars with each other, indirectly if not directly. Making the situation more perilous is the introduction of Artificial Intelligence-powered tools into warfare. [4]
For 60 years, one modicum of moderation came from arms control arrangements that constrained competition between the two largest nuclear weapons powers. But the last such treaty, the New START Treaty, which imposed limits on how many strategic nuclear weapons the United States and Russia could deploy, expired in February of this year. [5]
Proliferation for “Defense”
Although Trump has talked about a new treaty, no replacement is being negotiated. Trump has also told U.S. military leaders to resume nuclear weapon testing. [6]
Nuclear weapon testing would allow the United States, and other countries like China and Russia that will likely follow suit, to develop more destructive or usable weapons. Exploding nuclear weapons will also produce fallout — adding to the radioactive burden experienced by communities in those regions of the world where nuclear weapons were tested in the past. [7]
None of this should be happening had powerful countries respected international law. According to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) that was negotiated in 1968, the five countries that had tested nuclear weapons already — the United States, the Soviet Union (now Russia), China, France, and the United Kingdom — were to disarm their weapons.
Although all these countries are signatories to the NPT, they have so far refused to honor their commitments under Article 6 of the treaty, claiming they need these weapons for their security. Thanks in part to their refusal, the NPT is fraying, with the last three review conferences ending in failure, including the most recent one in 2026. [8]
When countries possessing immense military power claim that they also need nuclear weapons to protect themselves, it should not be surprising that leaders in other countries, with less military capacity, start mirroring this notion.
In June 2026, three years after joining NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization), the parliament of Finland voted to allow the country to “receive, transport and otherwise facilitate the movement of nuclear weapons on its territory.” [9]
Officials in Poland, too, have been expressing an interest in hosting nuclear weapons,[AP News, April 22, 2024, “Finland Tears up Nuclear Weapons Ban in NATO Shift,”.]] with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying that the country seeks “as much autonomy as possible” and will “eventually” seek its own weapons. [10]
A Nuclear Energy Connection
Then there are countries like Saudi Arabia that seek nuclear weapons, but through a seemingly more benign route: developing a nuclear power program. Such countries often claim they want nuclear reactors because of interest in developing sustainable energy or solving climate change. [11]
In September 2025, for example, the Saudi Minister of Energy declared that “the Kingdom is moving towards utilizing nuclear energy and its radiation applications for peaceful purposes… including the construction of the first nuclear power plant in the Kingdom to achieve multiple objectives” including “advancing sustainable development.” [12]
Although hardly known for its interest in sustainability, the Trump administration has promised “a decades-long, multi-billion-dollar nuclear energy partnership” between the two countries, with the assurance “that all cooperation will be conducted in a manner consistent with strong nonproliferation standards.” [13]
But reading the nuclear cooperation agreement signed in July 2026 by U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Minister of Energy Abdulaziz bin Salman, it turns out that the agreement might allow Saudi Arabia to develop the capability to enrich uranium.
The hypocrisy is striking: Iran has developed exactly the same capacity for itself, yet the United States sanctioned and bombed that country. Trump later flipped and his Truth Social post announced that there “will be no enrichment of material.” [14]
Saudi Arabia’s purported interest in sustainability makes little sense: solar energy has become the cheapest source of electricity, especially in sun-drenched Saudi Arabia. [15]
To understand what else might be motivating the interest in nuclear, one can turn to a March 2018 interview on CBS, when Saudi Prince Mohammed bin Salman pointed to the possibility that Iran might develop a nuclear bomb, and declared Saudi Arabia “will follow suit as soon as possible.” [16]
Developing a nuclear bomb “as soon as possible” is very likely the real driver for Saudi interest in nuclear energy. This is a well-trodden path; other countries have produced the wherewithal for a nuclear weapon by first developing the capacity to generate nuclear energy.
India, for example, set up its Atomic Energy Commission in 1948 for “peaceful” purposes but tested its first nuclear weapon in 1974, and then a range of weapons in 1998. [17]
So, too, Saudi Arabia might get closer to possessing the capacity to make nuclear weapons if it were to set up a nuclear program, regardless of where Trump lands on over allowing uranium enrichment.
Iran has become the poster child for this blurry line between nuclear power and nuclear weapons. The United States and Israel have used a potentially specious claim that Iran is developing nuclear weapons under the guise of a civilian nuclear program to justify their pitiless bombardment of that country and its population.
In fact, the White House listed 74 incidents when Donald Trump stated that Iran could not have nuclear weapons. [18] Benjamin Netanyahu can doubtlessly put up an even longer list, with his repeated announcements that Iran was weeks or months away from possessing a bomb, for three decades now. [19]
These atrocities were both ironically and hypocritically carried out by two countries that themselves possess large numbers of nuclear weapons.
Investing in Forever Arsenals
The United States and Israel not only possess nuclear weapons, they are investing immense amounts of resources — financial, material, and intellectual — to maintain or expand their arsenals. So too are the others belonging to the vile group of countries that possess this most destructive of weapons.
Between them, the nine nuclear-armed states spent close to $119 billion in 2025 on their nuclear arsenals, with the United States leading this perverse list by a wide margin. Its $69.2 billion was over five times China’s expenditure of $13.5 billion; the United Kingdom came close behind China at $12.6 billion. [20]
These activities come at the cost of essential social programs aimed at goals like access to affordable health care, which are being gutted in many of these countries.
Profiting from these activities are various corporate entities. A 2025 report by the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons (ICAN) lists 24 companies around the world with large contracts to contribute to the production of nuclear weapons, led by Northrop Grumman and General Dynamics “with outstanding contracts with a potential value of at least $31 billion and $24 billion respectively.”
Other companies include Airbus, BAE Systems, Bharat Dynamics, Boeing, China Aerospace Science and Technology, Fluor, Honeywell, Jacobs Solutions, L3 Harris, Leonardo, Lockheed Martin, Rolls-Royce, RTX (formerly Raytheon), and Safran. [21]
There is a strong overlap between the companies listed above and the arms manufacturing companies that have “provided Israel with weapons and other military equipment used in its attacks on Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon, and Syria since October 2023.” [22]
The other overlap is between this list of companies involved in nuclear weapons production and companies involved in the nuclear energy industry; entities like Fluor, Jacobs, and Rolls-Royce are in the business of selling nuclear reactor technology and producing nuclear weapons. [23]
In January 2025, for example, Rolls-Royce received a £9 billion contract to support the United Kingdom’s nuclear submarines while also being selected by the U.K. government to build small modular nuclear reactors. [24]
Risk of War, and Reactions
Nuclear weapons are not just ways for private companies to profit; their existence automatically gives rise to the possibility that they could be used. During earlier periods of concern about nuclear weapons, use was seen to be more likely a result of accidents or miscalculation. [25]
Today, however, explicit threats to use nuclear weapons to achieve political goals have become commonplace. Russian officials, including Dmitry Medvedev, have threatened nuclear strikes in Ukraine, and Israeli officials, such as Amihai Eliyahu, have suggested using nuclear weapons in Gaza. [26]
Trump has frequently threatened countries like North Korea and Iran. These leaders have already shown a willingness to inflict mass civilian casualties through conventional means. So, it is not inconceivable that one of these days, they might indeed use a nuclear weapon.
One reaction to blatant U.S. aggression has been to explain away, if not advocate for, other countries acquiring nuclear weapons — even among some sections of the left. [27] The argument often rests on the differential treatment meted out to North Korea or China or Russia, by the United States, which is then attributed to these countries possessing nuclear weapons. [28]
After the invasion of Iraq, too, some claimed that had Iraq possessed nuclear weapons, then the United States would not have attacked the country. But are such claims valid?
Excep

articles.title: Guns, Growth, and the German Reinvention of Military Keynesianism - War on the Rocks
articles.summary: Guns, Growth, and the German Reinvention of Military Keynesianism  War on the Rocks
articles.full_text:
Join War on the Rocks and gain access to content trusted by policymakers, military leaders, and strategic thinkers worldwide.
In March 2025, Germany did more than loosen a fiscal rule. It fused two national emergencies — a deteriorating European security order and a deteriorating industrial model — into a single constitutional bargain. The reform de facto exempted German defense expenditure from any domestic budgetary ceiling — as the German Bundesbank itself has acknowledged — and enabled a military expansion of extraordinary proportions. E.U. debt rules of 3 percent of GDP for annual government deficits and 60 percent for public debt technically still apply — though 14 out of the 27 Eurozone countries are not expected to meet these rules in 2026. The European Union is also in the process of loosening them. During 2025 to 2028, a Eurozone country with an approved defense escape clause can get away with a 4.5 percent annual deficit if its other fiscal commitment conditions are met.
Germany spent 46.6 billion euros ($55 billion) on defense in 2021. In 2025, that amount grew to 86.5 billion euros ($97.8 billion) — 62.4 billion in the regular Defense Ministry budget plus 24.1 billion from the Bundeswehr special fund. For the period 2026 to 2030, Germany’s draft budget foresees defense spending of roughly 750 billion euros. France is projected to spend 338.2 billion euros in the same period — less than half of the German amount.
The conventional explanation points to Russian military aggression and doubts about American support for European allies as the key drivers of this monumental turnaround. But this is only half of the story. The much less discussed part is Berlin’s attempt to use this vast, deficit-financed military expansion to revive its stagnating economy — an extraordinary experiment in military Keynesianism.
The spending measure that passed the German Bundestag by 512 votes to 206 was packed with pork barrel payoffs for almost every voting member of Germany’s mainstream parties — the Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union, the Social Democratic Party, and the Greens — with only the small liberal Free Democratic Party and extremist parties such as the far-right Alternative for Germany, the far-left Die Linke, and its offshoot Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht opposing it. Indeed, the amendment was passed by an outgoing Bundestag whose successor had already been elected. The 20th Bundestag met in a special session on March 18, 2025, after the February election but before the new chamber convened on March 25. This timing was consequential: The mainstream parties still commanded the two-thirds majority needed to amend the Basic Law. In the incoming parliament, they would fall short of that threshold, while Alternative for Germany and Die Linke would together have enough seats to block an amendment if both opposed it.
Individual lawmakers from all four opposing parties unsuccessfully sought to halt the proceedings through emergency applications to the Federal Constitutional Court. The agreement was therefore secured within the narrow window between the election and the new parliament’s first sitting, by a chamber containing 333 members who would not return. Although the outgoing Bundestag retained its full constitutional authority, as the court confirmed, the deal was concluded before the new balance of power established by the election formally took effect.
The key to understanding the breadth of the coalition supporting this spending hike is the economic shock for which its conventional policy repertoire offers no easy answer: the so-called “China Shock 2.0.”
The first China shock followed China’s entry into the World Trade Organization and primarily damaged relatively labor-intensive American industries such as textiles, furniture, and basic metals. Now it is Europe’s turn. China has built enormous industrial overcapacity. Domestic Chinese demand is too weak to absorb this output. Chinese companies therefore increasingly depend on foreign markets — above all the comparatively open and affluent European market — to sell their excess production. Chinese competitiveness is thereby not simply the result of superior efficiency. The International Monetary Fund estimates that the renminbi’s undervaluation ranges from roughly 16 percent to as much as 30 percent. The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development found that, between 2005 and 2024, Chinese firms received on average three to eight times more government support than firms in member countries of the organization.
China’s surplus in manufacturing is hitting at Europe’s technological core: automotive manufacturing, machinery, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and green energy. Germany is already shedding roughly 10,000 industrial jobs a month.
The industries most exposed to Chinese competition overlap with many of the capabilities required for military rearmament: precision engineering, vehicles, propulsion, optics, electronics, software, machine tools, and advanced materials. German defense expenditure can therefore be understood as an industrial conversion mechanism. It creates a politically legitimate source of long-duration demand for sectors facing shrinking civilian markets, preserves skilled labor and supplier networks, and offers firms a bridge from automobiles and capital goods into armored vehicles, missiles, satellites, and military communications. A crucial question is whether the bulk of these investments will simply rebuild previous strengths rather than replacing dependence on U.S. suppliers of advanced technology systems.
Logrolling describes a process in which groups with different concentrated interests trade support: Each obtains the policy it values most, the programs are bundled, and the diffuse costs are shifted to society at large. A heterogeneous coalition can agree on a policy package for different reasons, producing a larger commitment than any component would have selected on its own. This process could in principle produce a politically efficient outcome by aligning innovative nascent industrial sectors with support from established interests. However, it could also produce waste and overstretch. Research on such diverse cases as the New Deal, the Marshall Plan, and Wilhelmine Germany’s coalition of “iron and rye” shows that logrolls can pave the way to successful reform based on Keynesian economic stimulus but sometimes lock in protectionist or imperialist coalitions.
The March 2025 settlement was almost a textbook example of logrolling. Security conservatives obtained an effectively open-ended exemption from Germany’s debt brake — a constitutional barrier used to limit the federal government’s structural budget deficit to 0.35 percent of gross domestic product, sharply restricting its ability to finance new spending through borrowing — for qualifying defense and security expenditures. The Social Democrats secured their demand that increased defense financing be accompanied by civilian investment: a 500 billion euro infrastructure and climate fund, with investment commitments permitted over 12 years, including 100 billion for the federal states and municipalities. The Greens secured 100 billion euros for the Climate and Transformation Fund within — not on top of — that 500 billion, an explicit reference to climate neutrality by 2045 in the fund’s constitutional purpose, and an additionality or Zusätzlichkeit safeguard intended to prevent the fund from simply replacing existing investment in the regular budget. They also obtained a broader security exemption covering areas such as civil protection and cyber security. The agreement could then be justified in the shared language of security, resilience, and national modernization, even though its constituencies valued different parts of the package.
This interpretation does not require a conspiracy or proof that ministers privately rank jobs above deterrence. Logrolling works precisely because motives need not be identical. Some elites can support rearmament because they believe Russia may attack NATO and the United States may no longer underwrite Europe. Others can support the same program because defense is the only form of fiscal expansion that can now be presented simultaneously as constitutional necessity, strategic prudence, and industrial policy. The security argument explains why the spending is legitimate. The economic argument helps explain why it commands such unusually broad support.
The logroll’s fingerprints are also visible in the composition of the spending, not just its size. Of the 222 billion euros in German defense procurement orders with a known supplier since January 2020, 55 percent have been placed with purely German companies. Another 30 percent went to German firms in partnership with, or hosting subsidiaries of, foreign producers. This marks a dramatic change from orders placed directly outside Europe, which spiked past 40 percent in the panicked months after the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022 as Berlin rushed to buy F-35 aircraft, Chinook helicopters, and Patriot missile batteries off the shelf. Such outside orders have fallen every year since as domestic industry — Rheinmetall, Diehl Defense, Hensoldt, Renk, and ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems — has picked up demands. This national bias has become a particular source of friction with France: Paris has criticized the fact that Germany’s rearmament is doing too little to build a genuinely integrated European defense industry.
