articles.title: How the Iran war is ruining Saudi Arabia’s plans - Vox
articles.summary: How the Iran war is ruining Saudi Arabia’s plans  VoxEverything is going wrong for Muhammad bin Salman  The EconomistSaudi Arabia’s Military Limitations Are Being Exposed by Houthi Attacks  WSJWhy the Houthis Are So Hard to Defeat  Bloomberg.comHow Saudi Arabia Created the Yemen It Fears  The National Interest
articles.full_text:
As the US-Iran war drags on, the damage is being felt regionally: Saudi Arabia experienced the worst attack in over a decade earlier this month, when Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi militia struck an airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh. The strike killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 others.
Saudi Arabia responded with missile attacks on Yemen, striking oil facilities, and the Houthis have launched more strikes of their own, targeting Saudi oil infrastructure.
The dueling strikes are the latest development in a decade-plus of conflict between Saudi and the Houthis, a political and military group that controls part of northern Yemen, which had been on pause until earlier this year after a 2022 ceasefire. But the Iran war, and Houthi affiliation with Iran’s network of proxy groups, mean the current violence has far-reaching implications for the US, Israel, and the global energy economy.
It also threatens more than just Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil industry: As Gregg Carlstrom, a Middle East correspondent for The Economist, explains, the attacks cut at the heart of the country’s project to evolve into a destination for foreign investment, travel, tourism, and more. On Monday, the country’s upcoming Future Investment Initiative was postponed until 2027.
Carlstrom, who is based in Riyadh, spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram how the attack has been received inside Saudi Arabia, why it comes at an especially bad time for the country, and how President Donald Trump might — or might not — get more involved.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Can you help us understand how the Houthis have such a presence in the country right now? Are they infiltrating the country? Are they already there?
They’re shooting from outside the country. They’re shooting from Yemen. The Houthis are a group that’s been around for a few decades. They were originally a local insurgency in Yemen that was fighting against the Yemeni government. They originate from the northern part of Yemen, but they were able to gain control of large parts of that country from 2014 onwards. Ali Abdullah Saleh, the longtime dictator of Yemen, was overthrown during the Arab Spring and the Houthis were able to seize a large chunk of territory.
They are effectively in control of most of the population centers in Yemen. They have received increasing support from Iran, which has provided them with weapons, with money, with know-how, and technical expertise. And they have used that to build an arsenal of drones and missiles, which they are using now to carry out attacks on Saudi Arabia.
And was there a particular reason they targeted the airport in Riyadh? Were they trying to send a message here?
If you listen to the messaging from the Houthis, they are trying to describe this as almost a like-for-like campaign, where you’ve had years in which the Saudi-led coalition, which invaded Yemen in 2015, has been imposing a blockade of Yemeni airspace, has been restricting flights in and out of that country.
And so the Houthis describe this publicly as being a retaliation in kind, but I think they’ve also just figured out that attacks on airports are a very effective way to cause economic disruption in Saudi Arabia. You prevent not just people from flying in and out but also, as we’ve seen disruptions to shipping via the Strait of Hormuz, a lot of cargo that these countries depend on for daily needs are coming in by air instead.
Carrying out these sorts of attacks, shutting down the airport in a capital city, is a very effective way for the Houthis to impose economic pain on the Saudis.
And I guess on some level it makes the country feel insecure. How is that making Saudi Arabia’s leader feel right now? What’s his response been?
It comes at a very difficult time for the Saudi leadership because they are supposed to be hosting a number of events this month where Saudi will be playing a role on the world stage.
There’s something called the World Petroleum Congress that is taking place this week [October 11–15], which is normally a big event that draws executives from top oil and gas companies. Many of them canceled their participation because of the attacks on the airport.
Then they are supposed to be hosting the [now-postponed] Future Investment Initiative, which is something often known outside Saudi Arabia as “Davos in the Desert.” It’s the sort of flagship investment conference that takes place here every year. It draws a who’s who of global finance.
For a country that is trying to diversify its economy, a country that is trying to attract foreign investment and make itself into a hub for finance and travel and tourism, these sorts of attacks are very detrimental to those goals.
And this is coming as Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and the rest of the leadership in the country is really trying to establish Saudi Arabia as the premier economic hub in the region. The stakes are really high for him right now?
They are. And just about everything that they are trying to do is being disrupted by what’s happened over the past few weeks.
If you look at travel, for example, the Public Investment Fund, which is the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, last year launched a new airline, Riyadh Air, which they are hoping will eventually compete with Emirates or Qatar Airways, the really big carriers in the Gulf.
That airline was just getting into regular operations this summer where they were growing their fleet, they were growing their network of destinations. And then suddenly this happens and their home base in Riyadh is shut down. They have moved some of their planes out of Riyadh to other airports to keep them safe from Houthi attacks. Obviously, it’s very disruptive for trying to build an air carrier.
In Riyadh itself, the financial district — this sort of long-planned attempt to set up a banking hub that might rival the one in Dubai — had just started to get going over the past couple of years, when you had banks and other financial services firms moving in there. Everybody who works there has now been told to work remotely for the foreseeable future because there is a concern about possible Houthi attacks against skyscrapers and the financial district.
Everything they are trying to do, from finance to travel to trade, all of it is being disrupted and threatened by what’s happening in Yemen.
What options does he have to reassure investors and the world really that he can protect the country and maybe especially his airport, where a bunch of the investment is focused?
The airport, I think, is going to be difficult to reassure people about. You can install additional air defenses there. You can move more batteries and more interceptors there, but at the end of the day, no air defense system is hermetic. There’s no 100 percent guarantee that you’re going to shoot down every incoming projectile.
As long as there is this ongoing war between the Houthis and Yemen and the Saudis, I think people might have ongoing concerns about the airport. You have to resolve that underlying issue to give people confidence.
Now, how do you try to resolve that? If you’re Saudi Arabia right now, you have two bad options. One is you keep fighting. You try to militarily defeat the Houthis or at least force them to accept a renewed ceasefire.
The other option is you cut a deal. You try to offer the Houthis some concessions that might encourage them to go back to the ceasefire. That’s going to be very costly for Saudi Arabia. I’ve heard that the Houthis are demanding probably billions of dollars of financial concessions where they would want the Saudis to offer some money for reconstruction and to pay the salaries of Yemeni civil servants working in Houthi-controlled areas.
If you are the Saudi leadership right now, neither one is really a good option.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has a pretty strong relationship with the president of the United States, who’s very sympathetic to Saudi Arabia and Saudi investment. Has he appealed to President Trump for help here yet?
He has. He’s done so repeatedly over the past month or so, asking not just for support with the Saudi campaign in Yemen, but for America to carry out its own airstrikes in Yemen. And the response so far from Donald Trump has been to refuse that.
For the US to get involved in a bigger way, there are some practical constraints at the moment where a lot of American military assets are tied up in the Strait of Hormuz trying to keep that open, keep oil flowing through the Strait. And so the response from Trump has been disappointing for the Saudi Crown prince. The US is providing intelligence support. It’s helping on that front, but it is not directly getting involved in the war in Yemen.

He said Ukraine was again receiving advance warnings of ballistic missile attacks, which were seemingly suspended last week by the White House. “Now it works. It’s great,” he said, adding that the US move would save lives.

The Ukrainian president said: “It’s very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic [missiles] is coming. So we are thankful to the American side.”
Witkoff will on Wednesday meet Russian president Vladimir Putin after what a US official called “constructive” talks with Zelenskyy in Norway. The US envoy would aim to “create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations”, a US official told Reuters.
The talks in Oslo took place amid the worst crisis in US-Ukraine relations since Putin’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. Donald Trump has bitterly accused Zelenskyy of failing to end the war and has said Ukraine needs a new leader.
On Tuesday Trump again suggested Zelenskyy was the main obstacle to an agreement. “We want Zelensky to make a deal. He can make a deal. He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office,” he said.
Trump also said he had asked Putin to release Stephen Hubbard – an American taken prisoner by Russian forces in occupied Ukraine – in a further sign of his growing public alliance with Moscow.
The US president’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined Witkoff and Zelenskyy by video for the talks. Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, also took part, alongside EU and British security officials.
Zelenskyy said he had held a “positive” phone call earlier with the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio. Asked if Ukraine was now losing the war, after recent hostile US actions, Zelenskyy replied: “Of course we are not losing. But we are losing people because of Russian attacks and time. It’s a pity.”
He said he had raised with Rubio restrictions imposed last week on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s satellite internet service. The slowdown has crippled Ukraine’s ability to launch mid-range drone strikes on Russian battlefield positions.
Zelenskyy said he had offered to stop Ukraine’s long-range attacks on Russian oil refineries – a key Trump demand – if the US provided Kyiv with Patriot missile interceptors. The Pentagon has blocked the delivery of Patriots to Kyiv paid for by other countries, leaving Kyiv more vulnerable than ever to air attacks.
Speaking on Tuesday, Zelenskyy also said he opposed a trilateral summit floated by Putin, which would see the Russian leader, Trump and China’s president, Xi Jinping, meet next month to strike a Ukraine deal. Zelenskyy would be shut out, the Wall Street Journal reported.
“There can be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in Oslo. He added: “If it’s about Ukraine and our future it can only be acceptable when we are at the table of negotiations.”
The Washington-Kyiv crisis began 10 days ago when Trump announced he was lifting US sanctions on Russian diesel, in an attempt to lower fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. He then announced an energy ceasefire, which Kyiv implemented for several days but Russia ignored.
Despite this, Trump has bitterly rounded on Zelenskyy. He has effectively positioned the US as Russia’s ally, favouring Moscow over Kyiv, to the dismay of America’s pro-Ukrainian European and British backers. The US’s peace proposals have largely echoed Russia’s maximalist demands.
The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, on Tuesday questioned whether US negotiators had been honest brokers in the peace efforts. Witkoff has held numerous meetings with Putin in Moscow, while so far visiting Kyiv only once.
“Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now,” Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin’s terms “because Europe has been supporting Ukraine”, Kallas said.
Tuesday’s talks came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of US politicians that he believed “some political decision has been made to slow down … support for us”.
US officials have denied this but have failed to explain convincingly why satellite communication services were curtailed or intelligence sharing temporarily cut off.
Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio insisted nothing had changed. He said Patriot interceptors were in short supply and were needed in other parts of the world, as well as for the US’s own defence. “There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine,” he insisted.
At least nine people were killed in Ukraine on Tuesday. They included passengers who were travelling on the Kyiv to Odesa highway. A Russian drone struck two vehicles, killing three people and injuring four. One of the victims was the driver of a shuttle bus, which was on its way from the capital to a military cemetery.

articles.title: The Fog of Tech
articles.summary: Mara Karlin, a defense policy expert, argues that war planners’ obsession with new technologies like AI and drones has the potential to make them blind to the realities of war fighting. Using examples from Gaza, Ukraine, and Iran, Karlin shows how this technology trap leads to false assumptions about the future of war.
articles.full_text:
At a time when debates about national security tend to be polarized along partisan and ideological lines, there is one thing analysts and policymakers across the political spectrum seem to agree on: the future of warfare will be determined by technology. Hypersonic missiles, quantum computing, drone swarms, and artificial intelligence have all been hailed as transformative technologies that will shape battlefields, remake strategies, and upend established military doctrines.
Without question, these technologies are already having a tremendous impact. In Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Ukraine, and elsewhere, every party with the capacity to employ artificial intelligence and autonomous systems has done so—in the air, on land, and at sea, and at times in massive numbers. And there is also no question that in order to maintain its status as the world’s preeminent fighting force, the U.S. military must ensure that it has the most sophisticated and cutting-edge capabilities available. To continue developing and operationalizing these technologies, defense planners should prioritize scaling and integrating them and developing innovative operational concepts to employ them. The risk of being overtaken by rivals such as China is real.
But an equally significant risk exists: call it “the technology trap,” in which policymakers develop a misplaced sense of certainty about how innovations will change war and what warfare will look like in the future, while not paying enough attention to the unchanging fundamentals of war. An excessive focus on the role of technology would be shortsighted and lead militaries in dangerous directions, especially if planners are highly confident about how new capabilities will develop and make decisions in line with that confidence—which will almost certainly be misplaced.
For war planners, faith in technological answers can obscure the most fundamental questions: Who kills, who dies, and who decides? In the post–Cold War era, this myopia has contributed to dreadful outcomes in Afghanistan, Iraq, Ukraine, and Gaza. In the decade to come, as U.S.-Chinese tensions persist, the fog of tech could help pave the way for a disastrous great-power war. Policymakers should worry less about getting the right technology at the right time and more about how fixating on technology might make them lose sight of the essential elements of war and find comfort in false certainty.
THROUGH A GLASS, DARKLY
More than 50 years ago, the military historian Michael Howard famously cautioned that future wars are unknowable. “I am tempted indeed to declare dogmatically that whatever doctrine the Armed Forces are working on now, they have got it wrong,” he wrote. “I am also tempted to declare that it does not matter that they have got it wrong. What does matter is their capacity to get it right quickly when the moment arrives.”
But Howard may have been a bit too sanguine about the costs of getting it wrong. For Americans, the paradigmatic example from recent history is how the U.S. military’s technological prowess in the 1990–91 Gulf War seemed to herald a new, high-tech American way of war that would guarantee victory in the post–Cold War era. Instead, Washington slowly and painfully learned that the technological advantages that beat Saddam Hussein’s regime could not defeat insurgencies in Afghanistan and Iraq during the post-9/11 wars.
Predicting the role of technology in future wars has become even harder today thanks to the speed, scale, and complexity of contemporary technological progress. In the past, transformative innovations tended to be expensive at their outset—in resources or personnel—or required specialized knowledge and skills accessible to only a few. Think of the combined power of the rifle, the railroad, and the telegraph in the nineteenth century, or fighter jets and nuclear weapons in the twentieth century. By contrast, many of today’s technologies have low barriers to entry: they are cheap to produce, and access to the knowledge necessary to make them has been democratized and globalized. Enemies today often face each other on more equal battlefields, making it trickier for war planners to understand when and for how long new tools will confer an outsize advantage.
 In Ukraine, fishermen’s nets are one of the most effective antidrone defenses.
Focusing too much on procuring the shiniest equipment also obscures the ways that high-end technology works in tandem with more basic tools. In the 2010s, defense planners failed to account for this dynamic when predicting future battlefields, which they believed would be dominated by sophisticated platforms. In 2017, a senior Pentagon official declared that the F-35 stealth fighter would be “a war winner.” The 2018 National Defense Strategy, drafted under the direction of Elbridge Colby, who now serves as undersecretary of defense, anticipated that a few primarily high-end capabilities—including advanced computing, artificial intelligence, robotics, hypersonics, and biotechnology—would “ensure we will be able to fight and win the wars of the future.”
Instead, what emerged were conflicts such as the war in Ukraine, which can be described as World War I meets World War III. Sophisticated Russian ballistic missiles wreak havoc on Ukrainian cities, as do precision-guided glide bombs delivered by fighter aircraft out of the range of air defenses. At the same time, however, highly lethal bombs are dropped by drones carried aloft by simple balloons, and one of the most effective antidrone defenses consists of fishermen’s nets (or similar netting) draped over security checkpoints, critical infrastructure, and, in the case of Izium, an entire small Ukrainian city. A sense of certainty that sophisticated tech would dominate battlefields represented a failure of imagination that has produced real-world consequences: a dozen years ago, few would have predicted that during a U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, cheap Iranian drones would assault soft targets in Gulf Arab states, as they have since February.
THE CENTER OF GRAVITY
An obsession with technology can obscure the precept that war remains a human endeavor. As the military theorist Carl von Clausewitz said almost two centuries ago, “War is not the action of a living force upon a lifeless mass . . . but always the collision of two living forces.” Technology can inadvertently make war appear mechanical and sterile. But the nature of war has not changed. Its language is violence, and technology simply offers new and different ways to communicate. Therefore, the fundamental questions of war remain salient regardless of technological change: What are the ends (particularly with respect to politics), the ways, and the means?
Perhaps the most perilous time for leaders to be distracted by the allure of technology is when considering whether to go to war in the first place.
They often mistakenly believe that technology will make doing so less costly in political terms, particularly if they assume innovations will help reduce casualties.
A fixation on the tangible and quantifiable advantages technology confers can detract from vital debate and discussion of the broader consequences of resorting to violence.
This dynamic likely influenced Russia’s decision to invade Ukraine.
Putin and his advisers believed that the Russian military was sufficiently capable thanks to a massive technological reform effort that began in 2009.
In the run-up to the 2022 full-scale invasion, Russian Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu proudly claimed that more than 70 percent of Russia’s military had advanced weapons.
Within weeks of the invasion, it had become clear this had conferred little advantage on Moscow.
The same goes for the U.
S.
-Israeli attempt to topple the Iranian regime in 2026, a decision shaped in part by the belief that the sophistication of the American military, particularly when compared with its opponent, made success almost inevitable.
In the wake of U.
S.
strikes on Iran’s nuclear sites in 2025, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth declared that the attack showed Tehran that Washington’s military capabilities are “nearly unlimited.
” In fact, the limits of those capabilities became glaringly obvious when the Iranian regime withstood the 2026 onslaught and even managed to close the Strait of Hormuz.

There are ways to avoid the technology trap. The first is to determine a clear goal before going to war. Planners must develop a theory of victory before a single shot is fired and then steadily put that theory into practice. These critical processes cannot be negated by or outsourced to technology. Before launching the 2026 war on Iran, the Trump administration failed to clearly articulate the operation’s goal, instead offering a shifting set of justifications and rationales and various descriptions of the desired end state. The hope seems to have been that technological wizardry would make it possible to achieve everything on a long wish list without having to prioritize or navigate tradeoffs.
To clarify goals, planners must identify what Clausewitz termed “the center of gravity” of a military operation: “the hub of all power and movement, on which everything depends.” This is where an opponent’s power originates, so it needs to be the focus of a military’s attention and resources. During the 1990–91 Gulf War, the commander of U.S. forces in the Middle East, General Norman Schwarzkopf, identified the center of gravity as Saddam Hussein’s command and control of his military. Accordingly, U.S. strategy focused on impeding Saddam’s ability to communicate with his troops and weakening the Iraqi military’s ability to execute orders—a state of affairs that helped convince Saddam to accept a cease-fire. "American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for almost two years," Kaja Kallas said amid rising EU-US tensions.
High Representative Kaja Kallas has sharply accused the United States of pressuring Ukraine to capitulate on terms exclusively favourable to Russian President Vladimir Putin, just as a new round of peace talks unfolded in Oslo, Norway.
"American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for already almost two years, one and a half years now," she told the European Parliament on Tuesday.
"Why Ukraine hasn't surrendered on Putin's terms is because Europe has been supporting Ukraine."
Kallas also argued that European presence was necessary at the negotiating table to "balance" the positions embraced by the White House, which have become increasingly tilted to Moscow's interests.
Relations between the US and Europe have worsened since US President Donald Trump struck a diesel supply deal with Putin and eased sanctions until April 2027 without obtaining any Russian concessions in return.
Trump has called for new elections in Ukraine, which are barred during wartime, and complained that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin. Zelenskyy, in turn, said he feels betrayed by Trump.
"I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate," Zelenskyy told Bloomberg in a recent interview.
Kallas raised the alarm about the latest developments as she addressed the Parliament in Strasbourg, where several MEPs complained Europe lacked a peace strategy.
"That is not true," Kallas said, referring to a document she had presented to EU capitals with demands that Europe should expect Moscow to fulfil in a future settlement.
"If Russia is presenting their maximalist demands and requests, we should put our maximum demands on the table to balance these negotiations, and also to send a clear message to Russia that for all of those things that they are interested in – lifting sanctions – Europe needs to be around that table because they are European decisions."
"We are not giving these things up for free because it is not only peace that could be there, but it's also that this peace is long-lasting and just," she added.
Kallas accused Russia of endangering the security of the Black Sea with its armed blockade, weaponising food supplies and trying to trigger a global famine. Romania and Bulgaria have recently reported Russian drone strikes off their territorial waters.
The High Representative also censured Moscow for refusing an energy ceasefire and ramping up its bombing campaign against Ukraine ahead of the winter season.
"Ukraine wants peace more than anybody because they have been under bombardment for already four years now, and the fifth year is going on," she said.
"And Europe wants peace. It is not right to say that we don't want peace. The only one who doesn't want peace is Russia. Let's be very clear-eyed about this."

articles.summary: Lawmaker reportedly loses leg as car ramming stuns Australia  NBC NewsHelen Haines: Brendan Nugent silent and emotionless as he faces court over alleged attack on Australian MP  BBCAustralian democracy is usually peaceful. But there’s a homegrown history of political violence  The GuardianSuspect in vehicle attack on Australian lawmaker appears in court as police probe motive  ReutersNo bail for alleged Helen Haines attacker as police chief warns of Austra...
articles.full_text:
An Australian lawmaker was in critical but stable condition Tuesday after being hit by a car in what authorities said was a deliberate attack, shocking a nation where political violence is extremely rare.
Helen Haines, a 65-year-old independent member of Parliament, was struck Monday by a white Toyota Land Cruiser outside her electoral district office in Wangaratta, a town of about 30,000 people in the southern Australian state of Victoria. She underwent surgery overnight after being airlifted to a hospital in the state capital of Melbourne, about 150 miles away.
Local media reported that one of Haines’ legs had been amputated and that she was fighting to keep her other leg. The Alfred Hospital in Melbourne did not respond to an NBC News request for comment on the reports.
Australian lawmaker loses leg in car ramming attack
Police charged the driver, who they said was a 43-year-old local man, on Tuesday with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said earlier Tuesday that according to eyewitnesses, the driver had passed Haines and then did a U-turn, hitting her as she was standing by the trunk of her parked car.
“It’s clear that there was a deliberate act here. This wasn’t an accident, someone, you know, just skidding off the road,” he told the Australian Broadcasting Corp., adding that the motivation was not yet clear.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told the network that witnesses had described seeing the driver reverse and then hit Haines a second time.
The suspect’s father said the family knew Haines well.
She was a “deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community,” Brendan Nugent’s father, Rod Nugent, and his partner, Christine Cunningham, said in a statement Tuesday.
“Helen has been our friend for more than 20 years and what happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” the statement added.
Political violence is extremely rare in Australia, where lawmakers are often out in public with little or no security and their accessibility is a point of national pride.
“It’s an Australian tradition to have a chat to a politician that you bump into at the shops,” Josh Roose, an associate professor of politics at Deakin University in Melbourne, told NBC News in an interview.
But threats are rising as political rhetoric becomes more extreme, officials and experts say, particularly since the Covid pandemic.
According to the Australian Federal Police, there were 1,067 incidents of threats, harassment, nuisance or offensive behavior against senior officeholders, parliamentarians and protected locations in the 2025-26 financial year, a 12% increase over the previous year and twice the number five years earlier.
In a 2023 study of Victoria state parliamentarians, 82% reported harassment and 85% reported threats of harm, said Josh Holloway, a senior lecturer in government at Flinders University in Adelaide, with female politicians more likely to face abuse.
Holloway said that Australian federal lawmakers, especially those in rural areas, typically work from “shopfront-style offices,” hold regular community meetings and attend local events without security.
Those practices may now come under scrutiny, “but reducing public access to their representatives can come with significant democratic cost,” he said in emailed comments.
Albanese said Tuesday that it was everyone’s responsibility to “turn the temperature down.”
“We can disagree with each other, but do it in a respectful way,” he told Australia’s “Today” show. “And that’s something that Helen Haines always was characterized by, was that respect that she showed to others right across the political spectrum.”
Albanese said later that he had spoken by phone with local barber Ricky Jefferies, who ran from his nearby shop to help detain Haines’ attacker in what Albanese said was “a great example of the Australian spirit.”
“I heard a loud bang, with no brakes. It was crazy,” Jefferies told reporters. “I just ran out the front to see what was happening.”
Jefferies, who said he removed a knife from the suspect’s pocket and pulled him out of the car, said a lot of people “just ran to help.”
Haines, a mother and grandmother who spent three decades working in rural health as a nurse and midwife and has a doctorate in childbirth, was first elected to Parliament in 2019, then re-elected in 2022 and 2025. Her family said in a statement that they were grateful for the “swift assistance of bystanders,” as well as first responders.
The increase in political threats in Australia follows a similar trend in the United States and other liberal democracies, Roose said.
“Australia always echoes what we’re seeing internationally, but sometimes slightly behind,” he said.
Since the pandemic, there has emerged a “level of extremist discourse that is unparalleled in Australian history,” Roose said, one that is highly influenced by politics in the U.S.
Australia, and particularly Victoria, had some of the strictest pandemic lockdowns in the world, which left residents feeling “imprisoned, but also disempowered,” he said.
Lingering feelings of resentment combined with the current high cost of housing, fuel and other necessities have contributed to a “deep hostility” toward the government, Roose said.
Politics in rural Australia, especially, have become “highly inflammatory,” he said, “because of the online space and the poverty and the desperation that, quite frankly, has seeped into these areas.”
Roose said the “paradox” was that the victim was Haines, who is not considered a polarizing figure and is “someone who’s grown up and spent most of their life in these regions.”
“It indicates, I suppose, the challenge facing democracies around the world,” he said.

The district is home to the state pipeline operator Transneft’s Nikolskoye linear production and dispatch station, a key transit node along the Druzhba oil pipeline, which supplies countries in Eastern and Central Europe.
The exiled news outlet Astra used eyewitness footage of the fire to identify the targeted facility in the Tambov region as the Nikolskoye station.
Nikolskoye receives, stores and transports crude oil and refined products, including diesel, gasoline, jet fuel and fuel oil. Its pumping capacity is estimated at 300,000 metric tons per day.

articles.title: As Houthis encircle Taiz, Yemen's Saudi-backed gov't faces disaster - Responsible Statecraft
articles.summary: As Houthis encircle Taiz, Yemen's Saudi-backed gov't faces disaster  Responsible StatecraftYemeni City of Taiz Running Out of Essentials as Houthis Close in  The New York TimesHouthis attack besieged city in Yemen that U.N. says is at ‘grave risk’  NBC NewsYemen’s Taiz faces deadly siege, as Shabwah death toll rises  Al JazeeraYemen war continues to force families from homes amid hunger and disease  UN News
articles.full_text:
Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, endured a siege from 2015 to 2017. Today, it is encircled again.
The World Food Program says it cannot reach more than 600,000 people in and around the city. The International Organization for Migration counts over 200,000 people displaced since the Houthi offensive on Yemen’s Red Sea coast launched in September.
Why this city, and why now? The Houthis, formally known as the Ansar Allah movement, draw their strength from the Zaydi Shia highlands of the north. Critics say their governing ideology rests on the belief that the right to rule belongs to sayyids, descendants of the Prophet Mohammad, a lineage to which the Houthi family itself belongs. The Houthis have long denied seeking to restore the Imamate, but in Taiz, which has for a decade resisted Houthi encroachment, that denial finds few believers.
Taiz has a long history of political activism and hostility to the idea of religious hereditary rule. Its poets and journalists supplied much of the dissident energy that toppled the Imamate in 1962, and its streets were one of the centers of the 2011 uprising against then-President Ali Abdallah Saleh. This gives the governorate symbolic weight disproportionate to its size.
Moreover, Taiz is significant for its geography. It sits at the hinge between the Red Sea coast and the southern highlands that shelter the city of Aden, currently the administrative capital of Yemen’s internationally-recognized government, which the Houthis struck last week with missiles. Houthi control of the surrounding mountains would make the government’s counteroffensive around the Bab al-Mandab strait far harder to sustain.
That counteroffensive, known as Operation “Dawn of Yemen,” was announced on October 5 by President Rashad al-Alimi, a native of the Taiz governorate who chairs the Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, the body that leads Yemen’s internationally-recognized government.
The stated aim of the counteroffensive is to recover the whole country from the Houthis, the capital Sana’a included. So far, it seems to have stalled in its second week.
Government forces, under heavy Saudi air cover, have retaken ground around Bab al-Mandab and Dhubab. But Mokha, the coastal prize the Houthis seized in September, remains in Houthi hands.
The Houthis hold a contiguous area and can shift forces and materiel between fronts with relative ease. Their opponents consist of numerous factions fighting under the government umbrella, each of which answers to different commanders with different political projects. When the west coast collapsed in September, Tareq Saleh, who heads the National Resistance Forces that held the coast, withdrew to Aden, where southern units initially refused his men entry. The southerners' wariness stems from the role Saleh's uncle, then president, played in the 1994 civil war, when northern forces overran the south and crushed their bid for independence.
Indeed, Yemen’s civil war was already heavily shaped by external forces. Today, it has grown even more tightly bound to the wider U.S.- Iran war.
Since July, the Houthis have declared a blockade on Saudi shipping and turned their arsenal on the kingdom itself. King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has been attacked multiple times this month, with 13 killed and over 300 wounded.
The Houthis also hit Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran last week, with fire spreading across several floors. Reuters estimates Saudi crude output ran below 7 million barrels a day for most of the first six months of the U.S.-Iran war, leading to $50 billion in lost revenue at current prices. The International Monetary Fund expects the Saudi economy to shrink by 3.3% this year.
Riyadh’s response has been aggressive in substance toward the Houthis but restrained in tone toward Iran, the movement's primary patron. Saudi Arabia says it has carried out waves of air and missile strikes on Houthi territory, yet Saudi officials largely stop short of naming Tehran.
The reticence is probably deliberate. Riyadh has every reason to preserve room for a deal between Washington and Tehran that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz and hopefully end attacks from Iran and Iran-aligned groups on Saudi soil. Iran is also the outside power with the most influence over the Houthis. If Tehran chose to press them to de-escalate, that could create space for a Saudi-Houthi ceasefire and talks.
Subscribe now to our weekly round-up and don't miss a beat with your favorite RS contributors and reporters, as well as staff analysis, opinion, and news promoting a positive, non-partisan vision of U.S. foreign policy.
In the meantime, the kingdom has few viable options to escalate pressure on the Houthis, who set the tempo of escalation.
Turkey and Pakistan have activated the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, but both describe their roles as defensive. Egypt’s President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi on Saturday asked parliament for authority to militarily support the kingdom, but stressed that “we are speaking only about defense.”
President Donald Trump recently noted that the Houthis were “behaving very badly” and suggested he may ask Turkey to get more involved. Yet, with midterm elections looming on November 3, a war on Iran that has dragged on for eight months without settlement, and oil prices climbing, another American campaign in Yemen is the last thing the White House wants.
Riyadh, short of options, has yet to offer a comprehensive strategy beyond punitive airstrikes on the Houthis and support for its Yemeni partners’ counteroffensive, which is faring poorly, as the siege of Taiz makes clear.
The best clue to official thinking is a recent column by Abdulrahman al-Rashed, a former editor of Asharq al-Awsat and a well-connected Saudi commentator. He answers those who argue that the world should simply negotiate with the Houthis, as it has with other rulers of Sana’a.
The Houthi project, he argues, “is fundamentally at odds with the very idea of the state.” He describes how the Houthis have used all concessions and pauses to re-arm and wage war, calling the group “yet another Iranian proxy in the region, not the nucleus of an ordinary Yemeni system of government.”
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman appears to share this view that the Houthis are not a group to be accommodated. Chairing the cabinet on October 13, he declared that the “terrorist Houthi militia will face the consequences of its heinous crimes and attacks.”
Tehran’s position, meanwhile, has been contradictory. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei says Iran will help mediate if both sides ask and denies any role in Yemeni operations. Yet numerous investigative reports demonstrate that Iranian advisers and intelligence actively enabled the Houthi capture of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
Though Saudi Arabia has not responded to the mediation offer, the foreign minister of Yemen’s internationally-recognized government, Afrah al-Zouba, rejected it, calling Iran a “party to the war against the Yemeni people.”
This is not a surprising response. Iran’s own hardline press betrays official neutrality, running headlines that celebrate Houthi strikes on Saudi airports and Aramco facilities.
One report in Kayhan, whose editor-in-chief is selected by Iran's supreme leader, refers to the Houthis as the “Yemeni resistance” and frames war in Yemen as a “twelve-year aggression of the Saudi-American coalition.” Moreover, an adviser to the parliamentary speaker, one of the key negotiators with the U.S., wrote that Iran would use “tools in the Strait of Hormuz, Bab al-Mandeb and beyond” to keep oil prices elevated.
More telling is the extent to which Tehran has adopted the Houthi vocabulary. Iranian officials describe the Houthis as “Yemen’s armed forces,” overlooking the Saudi-backed government that holds Yemen’s U.N. seat, and call Saudi restrictions on flights and ports in Houthi-held territory a “blockade.” Riyadh sees those measures as the enforcement of a U.N.-backed arms embargo and as support for Yemen’s recognized government, whose current executive council took shape under Saudi sponsorship in 2022, after Riyadh pressed the previous president to step aside and transfer his powers to the newly created governing council.
Iran thus arrives with its position on the central questions already fixed, rendering its mediation offers largely hollow. Any Saudi move to the table would look like a concession to the Houthis’ and Tehran’s framing. That makes talks harder for Riyadh, even if it wanted them.

Seventh day of violent clashes between Albanian protesters and police
Protesters in Albania have fought with riot police on the seventh consecutive day of violent clashes.
The protesters, many of them high school and university students, are trying to oust embattled Prime Minister Edi Rama. Official figures said 295 people have been injured, 186 of whom are police officers, before Monday's violence.
"The moment the state negotiates with this," Rama told grim-faced police chiefs, brandishing a rock hurled at police on Sunday, "the state has fallen".
A police station and government buildings in Tirana have been attacked during the protests, which are being driven by demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and calls for Rama's resignation.
The protesters included "young men and women who have been radicalised by dark forces in Europe and the US", Rama said. "Albania has become one of the targets of a well co-ordinated attack."
In brilliant October sunshine in Rinia Park, also known as Youth Park, I watched people prising loose cobble stones - like that brandished by the prime minister - as ammunition for later battles with police. They did not have long to wait.
A convoy of police vehicles advanced down a broad boulevard, led by an armoured truck firing water cannon and tear gas canisters among the fleeing protesters.
Squads of riot police chased the predominantly student crowd through the park. Protesters took refuge in a cafe where even the eyes of the waiters streamed from the teargas.
Under trees, volunteers in yellow reflector jackets stood their ground helping those overcome by the fumes. I watched a young man remonstrating with a policeman, who then fired pepper spray in his face at point-blank range.
"The police actions are often chaotic and stupid," human rights lawyer Gentian Sejrani told the BBC. He provides legal support to more than 100 people who have been arrested.
"In court, the police rarely present evidence," he said. His clients include a man arrested on his way to a bus stop – completely unrelated to the protests, he said.
"Those who are actually throwing stuff at the police rarely get caught, because they run the fastest," Serjani said.
Police appear as incensed by the violence against their colleagues as the protesters are by the strong-arm tactics of the police. The result is mayhem.
Outside the cafe in the park, when the gas has cleared, 27-year-old activist Sidorela Vatnikaj, a masters student, describes her typical day. In a movement without leaders she is one of the more experienced, with eight years in the forefront of anti-government protests behind her.
"In the morning, you try to co-ordinate with all the groups - where they are, and where the protest is taking place. If any lawyers are needed, if any first aid kit or any kind of equipment is needed. And you also have to make sure all your friends, your family members in the protest are OK."
The day is spent going from protest to protest, much of it running from police, she said.
She is uncomfortable with the violence towards the authorities from her fellow protesters, but blames the police for starting and fuelling it.
"When I see people throwing stones at the police, I understand their anger. I don't judge them. I'm not happy, but they have no other way to be listened to," Vatnikaj said.
"They come from families whose family members had no other choice than to leave the country - a million in the past decade. They have not only been robbed, they have been bullied, ignored and now they they have also been beaten up."
At the weekend, the prime minister asked rhetorically what would happen if he stepped down.
"We need a technocratic government for one year, to prepare the country for real, democratic elections," Vatnikaj replies. She has accused Rama of rigging previous elections, and of being hand in glove with rich foreign investors and organised crime groups.
Young people in Albania feel encouraged by their fellow Gen Z protesters around the world, Vatnikaj said.
"I have seen my mother and father's generation, working all their lives and dreaming of having a democratic society where they could live with dignity. That never happened," she said.
Rama has been in power for 13 years, and has been a dominant figure in Albanian politics since the turn of the century. He has promised EU membership by 2030, and said he is the only one who can deliver it.

North Korea is considering restarting loudspeaker broadcasts near the border with South Korea, according to state-owned media.
Kim Yo Jong, the sister of Kim Jong Un, said in a statement to Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) that the country is also mulling over the decision to deploy “additional tactical weapons”. No further details on what this would look like have been announced.
The ramped-up retaliation comes as the country’s dictator says that anti-North Korea confrontation has “exceeded” that of the previous Yoon government.
North Korea could restart loudspeaker broadcasts
North Korea started dismantling some of its loudspeakers in August, following Seoul’s own removal of propaganda speakers a week before.
The move was described as a concerted effort to de-escalate tensions from South Korea’s liberal president, Lee Jae Myung.
But Kim Yo Jong told state-media on Monday that the situation on the inter-Korean border is now “very unstable”.
This isn’t the first time that the two countries have returned to using loudspeaker broadcasts to disrupt citizens and blare out propaganda.
After a six-year pause, the technique resumed in June 2024 in response to Pyongyang's campaign of sending rubbish-filled balloons to the South.
North Korea tends to play general noises such as sirens and drums, as well as howling animal cries – while South Korea has aired K-pop songs and news reports, striking a nerve for Pyongyang who is notorious for its extreme sensitivity to any external criticism.
Residents living along the border had complained that their lives had been blighted by loud noise coming from both sides in the day and even at night.
Seoul previously claimed the broadcasts could be heard as much as six miles across the border in the day and more than double that length at night.
North Korea’s AI torpedo
On Saturday, North Korea claimed to have successfully conducted an underwater test of a new high-speed torpedo mechanism that uses artificial intelligence for target detection and guidance.
The test-firing of Zam-2.0, a "super-speed, precisely guided" system took place on Thursday and heralded a “significant” change in Pyongyang’s naval capabilities, reported the Korean Central News Agency, without providing more details on the weapon’s use of artificial intelligence.
The state media report framed the test as a final operation to confirm the viability of the weapon's propulsion systems, following more than 180 evaluations over the past five years.

“As Serbians prepare to go to the polls on October 25, we stand for their right to make their voices heard in free and fair conditions and urge all parties to respect the vote count and relevant processes for verifying electoral results. Robust democracy in Serbia is essential for each of those goals.

“The Black Sea is the most important maritime artery for global grain, energy resource, and industrial goods exports, so its stability is vital for international food and energy security. We’ve informed our allies and EU partners about this. Our armed forces have prepared for intensified hybrid interference attempts and will continue prioritizing air defense and maritime security issues,” Romania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated.
But drone incursions are no longer the only threats to NATO countries. In Lithuania, unidentified individuals attempted to set fire to a facility storing Starlink satellite communication equipment. The sabotage attempt was prevented, since intelligence services warned the company of the threat in advance and strengthened security. Experts emphasize that such provocations by the Kremlin only strengthen anti-Russian sentiment in Europe.
“It’s precisely these senseless provocations, explosions, and terrorist acts that, on the contrary, turn people against them [Russia, ed.]. That is, ordinary citizens’ opinions start to change. They’ll start thinking: ‘Oh. It’s not gas we need from this crazy Kremlin old man, it’s protection from him that we need, because he’s aggressive, damn it,'” noted political scientist Peeter Taim.
Railways, logistics centers, and routes for supplying Western weapons to Ukraine — all of this could become targets of new Russian sabotage in Poland. The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) warns that Moscow could significantly expand the scale of hybrid attacks as early as this winter. Administrative buildings, civilian infrastructure, and transport hubs near the Ukrainian border are also at risk. Analysts don’t rule out new drone strikes either. According to ISW’s assessment, through this the Kremlin may be trying to disrupt the supply of Western aid to Ukraine, while also forcing European allies to focus on defending their own territory.
“Russia evidently views Western support for Ukraine as justification for its ability to carry out such actions on EU and NATO territory. At the same time, it wants to avoid direct military confrontation, I believe, with NATO and the European Union, because it lacks the resources for direct confrontation,” expressed Andreas Umland, research fellow at the European Policy Institute in Kyiv.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has also openly warned of the threat of new large-scale escalation. And this isn’t just political speculation, but data from Polish, Ukrainian, and NATO allied intelligence services. According to the head of the Polish government, the situation could seriously worsen as early as before Christmas. Tusk called for preparing for new acts of sabotage and provocations, which could prove significantly larger in scale than previous ones.
“We can expect further escalation before Christmas. Winter will be very difficult, especially regarding borders, railway lines, and everything on the Ukrainian side that could be used to transport gas, oil, and food. These attacks will undoubtedly intensify, and we should expect attempted sabotage or provocations on Polish territory — similar to what we’ve seen so far, but on a larger scale,” the Polish prime minister stated.
Meanwhile, Russia is replenishing its stockpiles of military equipment near NATO borders. Tanks, armored personnel carriers, and artillery are reappearing at storage bases that had emptied during the years of war against Ukraine. This is shown by satellite imagery examined by OSINT analysts. In Kostroma region, around 500 km from the Baltic states, new T-90M tanks and BMP-3 infantry fighting vehicles were spotted. And in Karelia, just 185 km from Finland, Russia is stockpiling artillery. For now, this concerns replenishing reserves rather than troops prepared for an offensive. However, amid growing hybrid threats, Moscow is simultaneously rebuilding its military potential as well.

Synopsis
India called for a universal and verifiable framework for nuclear disarmament at the UN General Assembly. The country emphasized that nuclear weapon decisions should remain under human control amid AI advancements. India reiterated its commitment to a no first use policy and a voluntary moratorium on nuclear testing. Legal assurances against nuclear attacks for non-nuclear states were also advocated by India's representatives.
Also read: Permanent India UNSC seat an 'obvious element' of global governance reform: Polish envoy
India's Permanent Mission to the United Nations highlighted Tewari's remarks in a post on X, reiterating New Delhi's commitment to global nuclear disarmament and efforts to strengthen the international non-proliferation regime.
"India acknowledges that the use of artificial intelligence in nuclear command and control raises real questions," Tewari stated. "We espouse the principle that the decision to use nuclear weapons should be taken by humans."
Reaffirming India's foundational defence doctrine, the delegate noted that New Delhi's strategic capabilities are purely defensive and shaped by regional security realities rather than targeted at any single nation.
"As a responsible nuclear weapon state, India maintains a policy of credible minimum deterrence with a posture of no first use and non-use against non-nuclear weapon states," Tewari declared. "We are prepared to convert these undertakings into multilateral legal arrangements. I wish to underline that India's capabilities are shaped by our unique security environment and are not directed against any specific actor."
Reiterating New Delhi's commitment to nuclear restraint, India reaffirmed its adherence to a voluntary unilateral moratorium on nuclear testing. Tewari also advocated for legally binding negative security assurances to protect non-nuclear nations.
"India believes that legally binding assurances to non-nuclear weapon states against the use or threat of use of nuclear weapons should alleviate their sense of insecurity, and thereby strengthen the non-proliferation regime," he noted, adding that such guarantees would directly contribute to reducing nuclear risk worldwide.
Underlining India's long-standing position on complete global denuclearisation, Tewari reaffirmed that New Delhi remains steadfastly committed to "nuclear disarmament that is universal, non-discriminatory, and verifiable."
"This goal can be achieved by a step-by-step process underwritten by universal commitment to an agreed, non-discriminatory, multilateral framework," Tewari explained. "We outlined this approach in our 2006 working paper to the First Committee, and again in 2007 at the Conference on Disarmament as document CD/1816. The relevance of this approach endures."
Tewari also highlighted two resolutions that India traditionally tables at the UN First Committee to promote nuclear disarmament and reduce the risks associated with nuclear weapons.
Convention on the Prohibition of the Use of Nuclear Weapons (Tabled since 1992): Calls on the Conference on Disarmament to negotiate an international convention prohibiting the use or threat of use of nuclear weapons.
"Such a universal legally binding agreement would build the political will needed for the total elimination of nuclear weapons," Tewari emphasised, soliciting continued co-sponsorship and support from UN member states.
Also read: India rejects report by UN human rights expert that says Indian youth face retaliation, terms claims as 'hearsay'
Clarifying India's position on existing international treaties, the statement noted that while the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW) does not impose legal obligations on New Delhi, India's broader commitment to global non-proliferation remains unchanged.
"The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons does not create obligations for India. Our commitment to global nuclear disarmament, nonetheless, remains unchanged, as does our commitment to strengthening non-proliferation," Tewari affirmed.
Concluding the statement, Tewari stressed the importance of international cooperation to prevent terrorists and non-state actors from accessing nuclear weapons, materials and technology.
"We also remain committed to promoting international efforts to prevent terrorists and non-state actors from gaining access to nuclear weapons, materials, and technology," the MP said.

In 1971, as the international monetary system was on the brink of collapse, U.S. Treasury Secretary John Connally told a group of worried European finance ministers that the dollar was “our currency, but your problem.” The dollar had become that system’s official reserve currency in 1944, under the Bretton Woods agreement, making signatories subject to the whims of U.S. monetary policy. Even after Bretton Woods collapsed and many currencies floated freely, the dollar continued to dominate. In the last half century, U.S. currency power has only expanded, as more countries have integrated into the global economy and therefore grown to depend on the dollar. China, reliant on export-driven growth, is foremost among them.
Reckoning with the possibility that Washington could someday make the dollar China’s problem, Beijing is now crafting its own solution. In a January 2024 speech, Chinese leader Xi Jinping made this effort explicit, instructing senior provincial and ministerial officials to accelerate China’s transformation into a “leading financial power.” A strong currency, he specified, was one of the essential foundations of that power. When Qiushi, the Chinese Communist Party’s flagship journal, published the full text of the speech in 2026, the standard Xi had in mind became clearer: for a currency to be considered “strong,” it must be widely used in international trade, investment, and foreign exchange markets and be recognized as a global reserve currency.
Xi’s call is the latest episode in a long history of efforts by major powers to reduce their dependence on the dollar-centered global financial system. In 1965, French Finance Minister Valéry Giscard d’Estaing famously described the disproportionate advantages that dollar dominance confers on the United States as “exorbitant privilege”; the same year, France began aggressively converting a substantial share of its dollar reserves into gold, contributing to the collapse of the Bretton Woods system. In 1999, the Japanese government released a report on how to promote wider international use of the yen. That same year, the launch of the euro gave Europe what would become the world’s second most important international currency, affording it greater monetary autonomy even as the European Central Bank carefully danced around any suggestion that it might challenge the dollar.
What distinguishes Xi’s ambition is that China, unlike Europe or Japan, possesses the economic heft, military capability, and political will to rival the United States’ geopolitical power. Not since London commanded a global empire has another country’s currency stood a realistic chance of competing with the dollar. A global financial transition from “In God We Trust” to “Where the Party Leads, We Follow” can no longer be dismissed as fantasy.
The internationalization of the renminbi would afford China a measure of financial survivability should the United States ever choose to wield the dollar as a punitive weapon, as it did against Russia after the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in 2022. The United States controls both the supply of the dominant global reserve currency and many of the critical financial infrastructure chokepoints through which it circulates. Washington, if it so desired, could severely restrict China’s access to dollar liquidity by making the cost of doing business with Chinese institutions prohibitive, for example by indicting or sanctioning a major Chinese bank. Any such measure would shock the Chinese financial system, raise transaction costs for trade, and deliver a major competitive blow to China’s export sector, which accounts for roughly one-fifth of its GDP.
Survivability, however, is only a prerequisite for credible deterrence. To deter the United States from using the dollar weapon, Beijing requires a financial second-strike capability. It must be able to redirect a substantial share of global trade and finance to a renminbi-based network. The durability of that shift depends on healthy global demand for an anchor asset priced in renminbi. For China, the most likely source of such an anchor asset lies in its dominance of the green economy.
Xi does not necessarily want the renminbi to replace the dollar. His 2024 speech advocated strength, not hegemony. Placing a respectable second, or even a consequential third, would suffice to break the dollar’s effective monopoly and constrain the United States’ ability to impose financial sanctions unilaterally, while saving China the effort and cost of sustaining currency supremacy. From Beijing’s perspective, the mission is to establish the renminbi as the Pepsi to the dollar’s Coca-Cola: never the market leader, but serviceable in a pinch and more than capable of keeping the dominant incumbent honest.
SECOND IS THE BEST
The near-universal acceptance of the U.S. dollar arguably benefits China more than any other country. The Chinese economy relies on exports, and Chinese goods priced and financed in dollars can reach ready buyers almost anywhere. The resulting profits can then be invested almost anywhere and converted into liquid funds on short notice. This suits Beijing: China enjoys the benefits of global liquidity without bearing the burdens of sustaining it. To preserve the global dollar system, the United States must tolerate foreign ownership of an ever-expanding volume of dollar claims as countries conduct ever more business in the currency. U.S. markets are exposed to international volatility, and foreigners hold some influence over U.S. corporations. The Federal Reserve, which issues the dollar, backstops the system, expanding its balance sheet during periods of financial stress, when governments and private companies hoard dollars to ensure they can continue to pay their debts and buy goods. This openness and exposure has posed little threat to the U.S. economy because foreign shareholders have generally sought to operate within, rather than change, U.S. business norms, and U.S. banks have earned tidy profits intermediating the world’s capital flows through New York and London.
China’s leaders have no desire to make any such tradeoff. Maintaining a global renminbi system would be fundamentally at odds with China’s state-led economic model. For the renminbi to replicate the dollar’s functions, China would have to create broad, two-way financial channels through which foreign holders of renminbi could reinvest that money into the Chinese economy. The resulting capital inflows would fundamentally reshape China’s domestic financial markets. It would be impractical for Beijing to confine foreign investors to a narrow group of approved assets, as it does now. Once foreign investors were allowed into China’s markets in force, they would arbitrage the distortions created by financial repression and politically directed capital allocation. Such competition would undermine one of Beijing’s most effective means of securing the loyalty of China’s business class: controlling who gains access to capital, on what terms, and for what purposes.
For many wealthy Chinese citizens, including some members of the Communist Party itself, the dollar is an indispensable form of political risk insurance. Domestic political rivalries can lead to asset seizure or even imprisonment with little due process. Offshore dollar deposits and foreign corporate structures allow elites to diversify their holdings across currencies and jurisdictions. Control of a company listed overseas, especially in the United States, offers wealthy Chinese more than prestige and access to global capital; disclosure obligations, duties to shareholders, and international visibility, which extend beyond the party’s control, can give Chinese executives leverage against arbitrary demands from officials at home. These constraints cannot prevent interference by senior authorities determined to pursue their targets, but they can raise its cost, slow its implementation, and create room for negotiation. The dollar-based system is a refuge for Chinese elites who fall from grace, and because no one’s position is ever entirely secure, few wish to see that refuge disappear.
USE IT OR LOSE IT
China is perfectly willing to go on living in a world that the dollar makes go round. But it cannot abide the dollar’s weaponization, and the renminbi still has a long way to go before it is strong enough to blunt that threat. If more countries and businesses are to adopt the renminbi, there must first be a global financial infrastructure for its use. China has already laid the foundation by facilitating renminbi use among firms in more than a hundred countries and across a growing array of commodity markets to settle transactions, obtain financing for trade and investment, and hedge their risks. Here, breadth matters far more than depth. Even modest daily volumes of renminbi transactions can keep payment channels operational, preserve financial relationships, and maintain the legal and administrative expertise needed to run an alternative financial system.
 Beijing requires a financial second-strike capability.
Because China’s relative economic strength lies in the flow of manufactured goods—it accounted for 20 percent of global manufactured exports in 2025—Beijing has concentrated its efforts on building a payment network that facilitates the commercial flows generated by its manufacturing machine. In 2005, Zhou Xiaochuan, then governor of the People’s Bank of China, publicly encouraged the already increasing use of local currencies among China’s trading partners. In 2009, the PBOC launched a pilot program for settling cross-border transactions in renminbi, followed in 2015 by the creation of the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, the backbone of China’s international renminbi network. articles.title: The Chokepoint Trap
articles.summary: The search for economic security will end in geopolitical calamity.
articles.full_text:
Policymakers used to ignore chokepoints. Now they have trouble seeing anything else. U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration warns allies against dependence on China while it hunts for ways to exploit those allies’ own dependence on the United States—on its market, technologies, financial system, and security umbrella. Beijing, meanwhile, accuses Washington of economic coercion while leveraging its dominance over critical supply chains to press the United States and Europe. Europe hopes to build the euro into an alternative global currency to evade the dollar’s iron grip. Smaller players, too, have gotten into the act, as Iran tries to leverage its control over the Strait of Hormuz to put a stranglehold on the global oil trade.
This obsession with wielding and countering chokepoint power may seem sudden, but it has evolved over the last quarter century as a byproduct of globalization itself. As economies integrated, chokepoints proliferated: manufacturers extended supply chains across borders, banks routed transactions through the U.S. dollar system to minimize costs and delays, digital services took advantage of economies of scale, leading the market to become dominated by a handful of platforms. After the September 11, 2001, attacks, the United States combined its advocacy for free markets with an increasingly ambitious effort to exploit its dominant position in these networks, surveilling global communications and using its influence over banks worldwide to cut off financial flows to its adversaries. But even as it did so, most politicians and business leaders continued to focus on globalization’s economic efficiencies.
Moves by Trump in his first term, however, caused world leaders to take more notice of chokepoints. The COVID-19 pandemic heightened countries’ fears of external dependence. Then, during Trump’s second administration, China learned that the best way to stop him is to squeeze a chokepoint. The United States’ hubristic erosion of basic norms of constraint led other countries, such as Iran, to explore options they had never previously dared to exploit.
Compared with an excessively rosy vision of globalization that emphasized the efficiencies of interdependence, it may now seem savvy to view the world economy as a system of chokepoints that countries can either turn to their advantage or see turned against them. But the chokepoint view has its own deadly blind spot. It is leading policymakers to focus on capabilities rather than strategy—to fixate on what leverage they have, and what leverage others have over them, rather than considering what happens when many countries build up their chokepoint power all at once.
The result is a familiar but dangerous dynamic: the security dilemma, in which one country’s efforts to secure itself make others feel threatened and respond in kind, leaving everyone less safe. The more that countries strengthen their control over chokepoints or protect themselves from coercion, the more they can make rivals feel that their own economic security has been undermined and provoke retaliation. As economic scholars such as David Bulman and Matt Ferchen have pointed out, each country’s individual actions contribute to the construction of a collective trap. The United States’ efforts to hamstring Chinese technology firms, for instance, led China to accelerate its technological development, which in turn spurred American fears of Chinese domination—a self-perpetuating spiral. Each side’s attempt to become safer makes others feel less secure, driving further escalation.
Escaping the chokepoint trap will be difficult precisely because it is collective. Any government that exercises restraint risks becoming a victim. And although the chokepoint trap may resemble the security dilemma, during the Cold War the measures that ultimately contained a runaway cycle of military provocations were implemented only after the deadly threat of the Cuban missile crisis focused leaders’ attention. An obsessive focus on chokepoints might lead to collective disaster, but it will be remarkably hard for states to jump off the escalator and balance making credible threats with offering credible assurances and seeking collective understandings. The most likely outcome is a fragmented world in which governments and private actors alike face increased volatility and the risk of escalation into something much worse: economic shocks, cascading disruptions, and even war.
ONE WAY RATCHET
In the traditional security dilemma, one country’s defensive move can appear offensive to another. A state may seek peaceful relations with a neighbor but worry that a belligerent leader could someday come to power next door. To hedge against that small but real risk, it might invest in a new weapons system or modestly increase the size of its army. Its neighbor could reasonably become alarmed. What if the buildup is preparation for an invasion? It may respond by ramping up its own defense spending, leading the first country to grow more suspicious and build up its military further, setting off an escalatory spiral.
Sometimes, of course, governments do have genuinely belligerent intentions. But even if all countries genuinely want peace, they can end up violently distrusting each other and seeking to field massive, expensive armies. In such a mistrustful atmosphere, innocent mistakes can easily be misinterpreted. In a classic 1978 essay about the security dilemma, the political scientist Robert Jervis argued that countries can mitigate the risk of misinterpretation by ensuring that the acts they undertake to enhance their security are obviously defensive rather than offensive—for example, by investing in fortifications deep inside their own territories instead of deploying troops to forward bases. But even passive defenses can heighten tensions: if a country feels better protected against retaliation, its rivals may fear that it will find aggression less risky.
In later writing, Jervis suggested that similar ambiguities might undermine economic and technological security, too. But economic warfare is even likelier to generate unintended escalation than the traditional security dilemma. Unlike military investments, economic policies can be difficult to classify as offensive or defensive. When China builds up its semiconductor sector, is it merely protecting its domestic economy or augmenting its capacity to coerce? Industrial policy can be enacted for a purely defensive reason—to establish resilience against geopolitical shocks. But if such a policy succeeds in building economies of scale, other states might reasonably fear that industrial dominance might be converted into coercive tools.
 Chokepoint warfare is a byproduct of globalization itself.
Economic security officials are usually more interested in building capacity than in restraint, whereas traditional economic policymakers are more accustomed to soothing their own markets than to assuaging the concerns of competitors, let alone adversaries. Defense bureaucracies have strong command-and-control structures for a reason: ill-disciplined communications and misaligned decisions can have disastrous consequences. The institutions that make economic policy, by contrast—including central banks and departments of commerce—are usually not set up to speak with one voice. Many are weakly coordinated, and significant authority is delegated to local-level investment and trade agencies. Sometimes, as with central banks, their autonomy is deliberately protected. Whereas military units deployed on discrete missions cannot act without explicit authorization, most economic agencies enjoy wide freedom to act without being accused of going rogue. As this year’s disagreements between the U.S. Department of the Treasury and the Federal Reserve over bond yields illustrate, standard bureaucratic infighting can shade into visible conflict.
When governments pursue chokepoint warfare, the problems these institutional ambiguities create get much worse. In September 2025, on the heels of a series of high-level economic negotiations between top U.S. and Chinese officials aimed at stabilizing the bilateral relationship, the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security enacted the so-called affiliates rule, which expanded export controls to cover more subsidiaries owned by entities on two U.S. government watch lists. The bureau publicly described the measure as an attempt to close a loophole and lighten administrative burdens; it has since suspended the rule. But the timing made outsiders unsure how to discern its broader strategic meaning. Was Commerce merely tightening the enforcement of existing export controls as part of an ongoing bureaucratic process, or was the United States, as Chinese officials suggested, deliberately engaging in “maximum pressure” tactics in between rounds of bilateral talks?
It can be even harder to interpret what autocracies intend, since policymakers in such regimes are more insulated from public scrutiny. For example, even after China promised to relax its restrictions on the exports of rare-earth minerals and magnets in July 2025, companies that applied for export licenses experienced unexplained delays. It was unclear whether China was deliberately signaling its ability to control critical supply chains or simply struggling to channel requests efficiently through a newly created export-control bureaucracy.
Governments engaging in economic warfare often intentionally write or enforce regulations ambiguously to prompt private actors to overcomply. This behavior makes others much more likely to interpret even hapless bureaucratic mistakes, delays, and unintentional overreach as malign and deliberate plotting.
